Most content is static, so serve it from a lightweight, single-purpose server segregated from dynamic content, allowing each to scale independently.

Apply performance and scalability patterns for their effects and costs: a service mesh sidecar offloads cross-cutting concerns at the cost of extra processes; a load balancer hides server failures and smooths latency but must be fast and is a potential bottleneck so replicate it; a throttler keeps services in a sweet spot but its logic must be fast; map-reduce parallelizes large divisible data sets only.

Build space-based architecture on four virtualized-middleware roles: a messaging grid routing each request to an available processing unit, a data grid keeping every processing unit's in-memory data identical via fast asynchronous replication, an optional processing grid orchestrating cross-unit requests, and a deployment manager that adds/removes units by load to deliver variable scalability.

Remember that space-based ('cloud') processing units and middleware can run on local servers rather than only PaaS, and that products vary widely in cost and data-replication capability — establish concrete goals and needs before selecting a product.

Expect the space-based architecture to rate high on agility, deployment, performance, and scalability but low on testability (high-load testing is costly and slow) and ease of development (unfamiliar in-memory data-grid tooling).
For every pattern under consideration, explicitly ask 'When would I NOT use this?' to surface the alternatives, since few patterns are always the right choice.
Choose an architecture from the specific problems of the system at hand; distrust any blanket 'always do this' advice because no single architecture fits all enterprise applications.
Treat each architecture problem as potentially novel and resist silver-bullet solutions, because prior blog or forum answers rarely transfer to your exact organizational context.
Choose architecture deliberately, because every system has one and letting it happen by default produces a Big Ball of Mud, so fatalism is not a strategy.

Structure enterprise applications into at least three layers — presentation, domain (business logic), and data source — using the lightest separation mechanism (subroutines, then classes, then packages) the application's complexity warrants.

Recognize that data-intensive applications are assembled from standard building blocks (databases, caches, search indexes, stream processing, batch processing) and match each need to the block suited to it.
Enforce the layer dependency rule: domain and data-source code must never call into presentation, so the UI can be substituted or changed without deep ramifications.
Keep domain decisions in the domain layer and let presentation choose only how to display the result (e.g., the domain decides whether sales are improving; presentation decides the colour or chart).

Treat mediating layers such as Application Controller (between presentation and domain) or Data Mapper (between domain and data source) as optional extras: start from the three base layers and add a mediating layer only when a base layer becomes too complex.

Detect leaked domain logic with the 'radically different layer' test: imagine swapping in a command line for the web UI or an XML file for the database; any logic you would have to duplicate has leaked out of the domain layer.
Weigh layering's costs against its benefits: extra layers cause cascading changes (a new field threaded through every layer) and per-layer representation transforms that can hurt performance.

Optimize performance through a disciplined, measurement-driven process: get the system running, instrument it, measure before and after every change, and treat all performance advice as unproven until measured on your own configuration.

Re-measure and re-verify optimizations after any significant configuration change (VM, hardware, or database upgrade), since such changes can invalidate prior performance facts or turn a past optimization into a regression.

Treat general performance rules as guidance only: always profile against your specific database and data and reserve dedicated tuning time, because caching behaviour and exceptions vary by environment.

Architect for performance up front (for example with an enlargeable resource pool) rather than fixing it afterward, and instrument the system by logging timing to find where time is actually spent, optimizing only the critical portions.
Use precise performance vocabulary — distinguish response time, responsiveness, latency, throughput, efficiency, capacity, and scalability — when stating performance goals or diagnosing problems.
Set explicit performance goals and benchmark candidate platforms on your own hardware and workload before choosing, because measured throughput directly sets machine count.

Use throughput as the performance measure for batch systems and response time for online systems, and distinguish response time (what the client sees, including network and queueing delays) from latency (the duration a request waits to be handled).

Specify performance requirements as scenarios whose event arrival is periodic, stochastic, or sporadic and whose measures include latency, throughput, unsatisfied-request count, jitter, and resource utilization.

For enterprise systems, prefer building for horizontal (hardware) scalability over raw capacity or software efficiency when adding servers is cheaper than adding programmers or optimizing for weaker hardware.

Treat portability as minimizing and isolating platform dependencies (ideally behind a virtual machine), variability as supporting a preplanned set of variants (especially valuable in product lines), and scalability as effectively utilizing added resources whether scaling out (horizontal/elasticity) or up (vertical).

Scale services by their tradeoffs: vertical scaling needs no redesign but is capped by the largest instance, while horizontal scaling runs multiple copies behind a load balancer (the maintain-multiple-copies tactic); make the load balancer the client-facing address so clients are resilient to instance count and address changes.
Pick the smallest set of tools you can while recognizing that different tools suit different purposes; a tool built for a different kind of application can hinder more than help.
Define the size and scope of the problem before building a solution, and do not default to the tool that is already there — match the tool to the problem.
Deliver software iteratively: release something useful to users as early as possible rather than waiting for a complete system, and actively simplify to turn a large project into a small one.

Build infrastructure and application functionality hand in hand through a walking skeleton that contains initialization, communication, data-sharing, resource-access, error-reporting, and logging but minimal application logic, growing it end-to-end to surface problems early.

Use your influence to ensure early releases tackle the most challenging quality attribute requirements so no architectural surprises appear late, and choose the right amount of up-front work at the project's sweet spot driven mainly by project size plus functional complexity, demanding qualities, volatility, and distribution.
Prefer a web presentation and adopt a rich client only when you must, because web front ends avoid client-deployment problems and are increasingly capable.

Treat presentation as relatively independent of the lower layers: prefer an HTML browser interface if you can get away with it and a rich client only if you cannot, with Model View Controller underneath, and pick controllers and views (Page vs Front Controller, Template vs Transform View) by site nature and team tooling.
If domain logic must run on the client, keep all of it in one place; never split domain logic across client and server, because you then no longer know where any piece of logic lives.

Keep request-specific domain logic out of the Application Controller: because the domain/application boundary is murky a few such cases may live there, but when the logic recurs in many places drive it from the Domain Model instead.

Keep all code in a single process (one node, or replicated across a cluster) and do not separate layers into distinct processes unless you absolutely must, because distribution degrades performance and forces extra patterns like Remote Facade and Data Transfer Object.
To use multiple processors, prefer clustering: put all classes in a single process and run multiple copies of that process across nodes, so every call stays local and fine-grained.

Treat distribution, explicit multithreading, the object/relational impedance mismatch, multiplatform development, and extreme performance needs as complexity boosters that each carry high build-and-maintain cost; adopt each only when genuinely required.
Treat reliability, scalability, and maintainability as the primary design goals even for mundane applications, and sacrifice reliability only as a conscious, explicit cost trade-off.

Expect to rethink the architecture on roughly every order-of-magnitude increase in load, because no architecture is one-size-fits-all (each is specific to its application's load assumptions), and avoid over-engineering for hypothetical future load since wrong load assumptions make the effort wasted or counterproductive.

Select the domain-logic pattern (Transaction Script, Table Module, or Domain Model) primarily by domain-logic complexity: Transaction Script for simple logic, Domain Model as complexity rises, since simple approaches hit a wall where each new feature gets exponentially harder.

Because domain-logic complexity cannot be measured numerically, make the structuring choice as an experienced judgment call from initial requirements analysis, and weight it toward Domain Model when the team is already strong with that approach.

Invest upfront thought in the domain-logic choice because it is hard to change later; if Transaction Script proves wrong, refactor toward Domain Model, but reverting from Domain Model to Transaction Script is rarely worthwhile unless you can also simplify the data source layer.

If you adopt a Domain Model, make it dominant rather than mixing in use-case (Transaction Script) controllers, because such controllers encourage duplicated code; you may still mix patterns deliberately where parts of the system are genuinely simpler.

Make the domain-logic approach (Transaction Script, Table Module, or Domain Model) the central enterprise design decision, driven mainly by domain-logic complexity and secondarily by the difficulty of the database connection.

Match the domain-logic pattern to complexity: Transaction Script for simple logic (its cost multiplies exponentially as logic grows), a Domain Model for genuinely complex logic (needs real skill and brings a messy relational connection), and Table Module as a relational-friendly middle ground (especially strong on .NET).

Understand Transaction Script as organizing all domain logic for one system transaction primarily as a single procedure that calls the database directly or through a thin wrapper, factoring common subtasks into shared subprocedures, with the benefit that each script need not worry about what other transactions are doing.

Watch Transaction Script's failure mode of duplicated code across transactions as business logic grows, and because refactoring a Transaction Script design into a Domain Model is harder than it should be, choose a Domain Model early when you expect the domain logic to become complex.
Use Table Module only when the environment supplies strong Record Set tooling (e.g., COM/.NET); with such tooling prefer it over Transaction Script, and without it do not bother with Table Module.

Separate database logic from a Transaction Script even in the simplest applications, choosing Row Data Gateway or Table Data Gateway, with strong Record Set tooling tilting you toward Table Data Gateway.
On .NET default to Table Module because the platform tooling orbits the data set acting as a Record Set, reserving Transaction Script for the very simplest cases.

Use Table Module to package data with behavior over a relational-friendly backing structure (a Record Set from a SQL call), letting its structure follow the virtual tables the application perceives (views and queries), not strictly the physical tables.

Implement a Table Module as an instance initialized with a record set rather than as static methods, which enables specialization through inheritance and lets you test it by building a Record Set in memory without going to the database.

Use a Row Data Gateway as an object that exactly mimics a single record (one field per column) and hides all data-source access, containing only database-access logic and no domain logic (domain logic would make it an Active Record); it pairs well with Transaction Script by factoring reusable database access.

Use Record Set together with Table Module when your environment relies on the Record Set as its common data structure: fetch a Record Set, pass it to a Table Module to calculate derived information, to the UI for display and editing, back to the Table Module for validation, then commit the updates.

Add a Service Layer as the application's API over a Domain Model or Table Module — a natural home for transaction control and security described per method — but keep it as thin as possible (or omit it), adopting it only when the application demands it.

Make a Service Layer operation responsible for coordinating and atomically transacting the application's full response to a use case (for example validation plus notifying other people and integrated applications), which can be far from trivial.

Separate all SQL access from domain logic into dedicated Gateway classes organized one per table, so SQL is easy to find, the rest of the application knows nothing about SQL, and database specialists have a clear place to work.

Match the persistence mechanism to the Domain Model's richness: use Active Record for a simple model that mirrors the tables, and Data Mapper for a rich model, since Active Record breaks down once one-to-one class/table mapping fails or you need inheritance and database-free domain tests.

Build the Domain Model without regard to the database — beware a model shaped like the schema — and treat the schema purely as a way to persist object data; use Data Mapper for maximum flexibility, or Active Record only when an isomorphic schema genuinely makes sense.

For a Domain Model choose the data-source pattern by complexity: Active Record when simple, Data Mapper (ideally with a mapping tool) when complex, and Unit of Work as the focal point for concurrency control.

Do not shield a Domain Model with a Row Data Gateway (three data representations is one too many): use Active Record for simple mappings and Data Mapper for complex ones, keeping Row Data Gateways mirroring the database structure.

Use Data Mapper to let the database schema and object model evolve independently (most commonly with a Domain Model, so you can ignore the database while designing and testing the model); because its price is an extra layer, gate on complexity: simple logic needs neither Domain Model nor Data Mapper, never use Data Mapper without a Domain Model, but a simple Domain Model over a developer-controlled database may use Active Record and refactor to a mapping layer as complexity grows.
Pick a single primary persistence mechanism and do not mix them, because mixing gets messy; a data Gateway may still wrap tables or services treated as external interfaces even under Data Mapper.

Budget object-relational mapping as a large, ongoing cost (anecdotally ~a third of programming effort that persists through maintenance), and seriously consider buying a mature O/R mapping tool for a Domain Model rather than hand-building the layer.

Bridge object references and relational keys with Identity Field, Identity Map, and Foreign Key Mapping: store each object's key, look up by key on read, and wire references from foreign keys, falling back to a database fetch or Lazy Load when the key is not already in memory.

Treat repetitive mapping code as a design smell: factor out the common behaviour or adopt Metadata Mapping (a metadata description driving code generation or reflection), which is why mature commercial O/R tools are metadata-based and enable Query Object and Repository.

Adopt a Repository to concentrate query-construction code in one place and minimize duplicate query logic (important with many domain classes or heavy querying), gaining a clean one-way dependency from domain to data mapping and a persistence layer that looks like an in-memory collection of domain objects.
Use an Identity Map to record every row read so the same row is never loaded into two in-memory objects; treat correct identity as its primary purpose and caching as only a secondary benefit.
Use Identity Field to store the relational primary key inside the in-memory object, maintaining the object-to-row correspondence required in order to write data back.
Use Lazy Load placeholders for object references so the real object is fetched only when the link is followed, preventing one read from dragging an enormous object graph out of the database.

Read efficiently: pull back multiple rows at once, never issue repeated queries on the same table, and prefer joins to load several tables together — but limit to about three or four joins per query before performance suffers.

Gather data from multiple tables in a single joined query (a multitable find) rather than one query per table, because each SQL call is a slow remote call; and when loading a referenced object from the join, check the Identity Map first so an already-loaded object is reused rather than duplicated.

Avoid the N+1 query problem (loading N objects when each needs a separate query for its association turns into N+1 queries, such as 101 for a hundred employees and their skills) by using a multitable join, but because that optimization is more awkward, apply it only where needed and spend your energy on the slow, important queries.

Prefer separate finder objects over static find methods so database operations stay substitutable (e.g., replaceable by a Service Stub in tests), and run queries at the start of a unit of work since finders see database state, not unsaved in-memory objects.
Prefer separate finder objects over static find methods on a Row Data Gateway so finders remain polymorphic and substitutable across different data sources.
Map a many-to-many association with a dedicated Association Table (link table), because a relational database cannot hold a collection on both ends directly.
Do not depend on collection ordering across persistence: use unordered sets or apply an explicit sort per query, since arbitrary order is hard to maintain in a relational store.

In a column store, impose a sort order an entire row at a time (never per column) to act as an index chosen from common queries, which also boosts compression by forming long runs on the first sort key, and consider storing the data sorted several different ways across the replicas you keep for fault tolerance so each query uses the best-fitting order.

Control write ordering for referential integrity: defer integrity checks to transaction end if the database supports it; otherwise order writes by topological/hardcoded table order to satisfy per-write checks and reduce deadlock rollbacks.

Avoid manually ordering updates for referential integrity by configuring the database to check integrity only at commit (most databases allow it, with no good reason not to); otherwise let the Unit of Work sort update order, and always edit tables in the same fixed sequence (held in the Unit of Work) to reduce deadlocks.

Separate the two requirements that consistency conflates, timeliness (an up-to-date view, whose violations are temporary and resolve by waiting) and integrity (absence of corruption, whose violations are permanent and need explicit repair), and prioritize integrity over timeliness in most applications because a timeliness lapse is merely annoying while an integrity lapse such as money charged but not paid is catastrophic; note that ACID transactions provide both but event-based dataflow decouples them, with integrity preserved by exactly-once semantics.

Where the cost of an apology is acceptable, adopt loosely interpreted constraints by writing optimistically and checking the constraint after the fact (compensating for violations through apology workflows) rather than checking every constraint before writing, which enables coordination-avoiding data systems that maintain strong integrity without atomic commit, linearizability, or synchronous cross-partition coordination, such as a multi-leader deployment replicating asynchronously across datacenters with synchronous coordination introduced only where recovery is impossible.
Embed small Value Objects (money, date ranges) as columns of the owning row (Embedded Value) and skip the Identity Map, because value objects have value rather than reference semantics.

Use a Serialized LOB to store a clustered object group as one column (e.g., XML) to avoid many small calls for hierarchic structures, but only when you never need to query the parts, and not so widely that the database degenerates into a transactional file system.

Pick a Serialized LOB form by trade-offs: a BLOB is simplest and most space-efficient where the platform auto-serializes but is binary, opaque to casual viewing, and most seriously suffers versioning problems when the class changes, while a CLOB is human-readable but larger, may need a custom parser, and is slower; XML removes the parser and standardization problems at a verbosity (space) cost, and a zipped XML BLOB trades readability back for space.

Beware identity and duplication with a Serialized LOB: do not embed a shared, updatable LOB (such as customer details) in another table (such as order), which copies the data per row; place the LOB in its own table so many rows can link to it, and ensure its data is reachable only from the single owning object, embedding it only when you deliberately want a point-in-time snapshot.

Use Serialized LOB only for a slice of the object model that will not be queried via SQL from outside the application, because it works poorly when outside objects must reference objects buried inside it, and its main disadvantage is that you cannot query its internal structure with SQL.
Note that structures suitable for a Serialized LOB are often also suitable for a separate denormalized reporting database, into which the LOB can be transformed into table structures.

Choose an inheritance-mapping strategy by trading data duplication against access speed: default to Single Table Inheritance for simplicity and refactoring resilience, and reach for Class or Concrete Table Inheritance as wasted-column or access pressures demand, mixing strategies only when justified and consulting DBAs.

For Class Table Inheritance, give each class its own mapper that handles only that class's table (chaining to the superclass mapper via base calls) with a top-level mapper dispatching by type code on find and by runtime type on update, insert, and delete; cache query results in an in-memory data set to access table data cheaply (or join across all the hierarchy's tables), and insert in two stages: create the blank rows, then let per-class save methods populate them.
Build the database incrementally inside each short iteration (six weeks or less) rather than deferring persistence for months, which risks crippling, expensive-to-refactor performance problems.

Treat database connections as expensive resources: tie each connection to its transaction (open on begin, close on commit/rollback), close as soon as you are done, and do not rely on garbage collection to close them.

Keep all data manipulation inside transactions so the transaction manager handles the most dangerous concurrency problems, but manage offline concurrency (across multiple transactions) explicitly, since no single system transaction can cover it.

Keep transactions as short as possible for throughput and, as a general rule, never let a single system transaction span multiple requests; open the transaction late (at first write) only when contention is heavy or business transactions span requests, accepting the inconsistent-read exposure.

Know what each transaction locks: too many row locks make the database escalate to a table lock that excludes everyone, so avoid a single shared 'object' table or Layer Supertype table that becomes a lock-escalation magnet.

Usually wrap a whole Transaction Script in a single system transaction, except when one request reads data for editing and a later request saves it, where Optimistic Offline Lock is almost always the best choice.
Verify that connection pooling actually helps before building it yourself, since most platforms already pool for you.
Make a connection available through a thread-scoped Registry rather than threading it through many method parameters, and never share one connection across threads.

Write robust SQL access: avoid 'select *' with positional column indices (use column names), prefer static precompilable SQL over string-concatenated dynamic SQL, and batch multiple statements into a single call in production.
Keep simple create/read/update/delete test cases for every database mapping structure to catch when the SQL drifts out of sync with the code.

Split request handling from response formatting with Model View Controller: use a script/controller to interpret the request and a server page to format the response, keeping domain models completely separate so presentation is easy to change and domain logic easy to test.

Have a Page Controller handle a request by creating the necessary model objects, placing the data the view needs into the HTTP request, and forwarding to the view (putting the common forwarding on a superclass), and recognize that its main coupling to a Template View is the request-parameter names used to pass objects.

Use Transform View to render the model's data into HTML as a transformation that walks the domain data and writes HTML per recognized element type, recognizing that, unlike an output-organized Template View, a Transform View is organized around separate per-element transforms dispatched by a simple loop, so its rules can be arranged in any order without affecting the output.

Add an Application Controller only when the machine controls screen flow and navigation order; you do not need one when the user is free to reach any screen in any order (test: machine-in-control ⇒ needed; user-in-control ⇒ not).

Use an Application Controller when there are definite rules about the order pages are visited and state-dependent view choices, and skip it when any screen can be visited in any order; treat having to make similar changes in many places whenever the flow changes as the signal to introduce one.

Keep programming logic out of the page structure in a Template View (delegate to a helper object), because embedded logic tends toward messy, unmaintainable pages; use Transform View when domain data is XML, and Two Step View only when screens share a common logical structure.

Avoid programming logic (scriptlets) in server pages, because a page is a poor program module that loses structural and modular features, blocks designers and nonprogrammers from editing it, and makes it too easy to mingle layers and duplicate domain logic; instead give each page a regular helper object holding the real logic so the page stays a pure Template View.

Choose Page Controller (one controller per page/action) for simple sites and Front Controller (single routing object) when you want centralized HTTP handling that absorbs changes to the action structure without web-server reconfiguration, and separate handling the HTTP request from deciding what to do with it.

Choose optimistic vs pessimistic locking by conflict frequency and severity: prefer optimistic (conflict detection at commit — better concurrency, easier to implement) when conflicts are rare or low-consequence, and pessimistic (conflict prevention) when a late-discovered conflict is painful for users.

Treat deadlock as the characteristic risk of pessimistic locking, and for enterprise applications prefer very simple, conservative schemes (e.g., acquire all locks up front plus a timeout), accepting some unnecessary victims, because missing a deadlock scenario is far worse and 'deadlock-proof' schemes are easy to get wrong.

Understand that Pessimistic Offline Lock prevents conflicts by forcing a business transaction to acquire a lock before using data, so once begun it is likely to complete, in contrast to optimistic locking where a victim does all the work only to fail at commit, which becomes unpopular for lengthy transactions.

Use Pessimistic Offline Lock only when the chance or cost of conflict is high, treating it as complementary to Optimistic Offline Lock and never locking every entity, which would create tremendous contention.

Prefer conflict avoidance as the simplest multi-leader strategy by routing all writes for a given record through the same leader so conflicts cannot occur, remembering that a single-leader database blocks or aborts a conflicting writer whereas multi-leader detects conflicts only asynchronously when it may be too late, and that conflict avoidance breaks down when the designated leader for a record must change.

Do not version-check every datum you merely read: distinguish data you only read from data you actually used to make a decision, accepting that classifying them correctly (e.g., a zip code that drives tax) takes careful analysis, to avoid needless conflicts and waits.

Set isolation level per transaction as a deliberate correctness-versus-liveness trade: Serializable guarantees correctness but harms throughput, so lower it (Repeatable Read, Read Committed, Read Uncommitted) only where the specific inconsistent-read errors that level admits are acceptable for that transaction.

Let the transaction system handle concurrency as much as possible, and take on cross-system-transaction control only when you genuinely must; for offline concurrency make Optimistic Offline Lock the first choice and switch to Pessimistic Offline Lock when a late commit-time failure would be too costly.
Detect inconsistent reads, when the isolation level is unknown, by registering read objects and incrementing their version during commit.

Use a transaction to group several reads and writes into one all-or-nothing logical unit that commits or aborts and is safe to retry, simplifying error handling, but recognize that not every application needs transactions (weakening or abandoning them can buy performance or availability) and that both the claim that transactions are the antithesis of scalability and the claim that they are essential for serious applications are hyperbole.

Do not trust an ACID label to tell you what guarantees you get, because implementations differ (especially the meaning of isolation), and understand that atomicity is really abortability, discarding a transaction's partial writes when a fault occurs so the application can safely retry, not a concurrency property.

Understand the rest of ACID precisely: consistency is an application-specific notion of invariants that the application (not the database) is responsible for preserving, isolation is formalized as serializability but is rarely used at full strength because of its performance cost, and durability is the promise that committed data survives a crash, which requires the database to wait for writes to nonvolatile storage or replicas before reporting a commit.

Understand the concurrency anomalies and how to prevent them rather than blindly trusting an ACID label, because concurrency bugs are hard to find by testing and to reason about, serializable isolation is the ideal but is often avoided for its cost in favor of weak isolation, and weak-isolation bugs have caused real financial loss and data corruption even in databases considered ACID.

Recognize read committed isolation as guaranteeing only no dirty reads and no dirty writes (preventing visibility of partially updated state and the mixing of conflicting writes, but not lost updates), typically implemented by row-level write locks held to commit plus remembering the old committed value so readers are never blocked.

Guard against write skew, where two transactions read the same data and then update different objects in a way that together violates an invariant, recognizing that single-object atomic operations and automatic lost-update detection do not help, that only true serializable isolation prevents it automatically, and that otherwise you must explicitly lock the rows the decision depends on; it arises in many check-then-act scenarios such as on-call scheduling and double-booking.

Handle phantoms, where one transaction's write changes the result of another's search query, by noting that snapshot isolation prevents them only for read-only queries and that write-skew phantoms require index-range locks or, as a last resort, materializing conflicts with precreated lock rows, with serializable isolation preferable in most cases.

Use serializable isolation when you need to prevent all race conditions, since it guarantees the outcome is as if transactions ran one at a time, and bear in mind that weak isolation levels persist mainly because isolation is hard to understand, inconsistently implemented, and hard to verify as safe for a given application.

Understand two-phase locking (distinct from two-phase commit) as providing serializability by having readers block writers and writers block readers, implemented with a per-object lock in shared (read) or exclusive (write) mode held until the transaction ends, so it prevents all the race conditions including lost updates and write skew.

Consider serializable snapshot isolation, an optimistic technique that lets transactions proceed without blocking and checks at commit whether isolation was violated, for full serializability with only a small penalty over snapshot isolation, recognizing that optimistic control outperforms pessimistic locking only when contention is low and spare capacity exists.

Understand that serializable snapshot isolation enforces serializability by detecting when a transaction acted on a premise that has since changed (stale MVCC reads and writes that affect another transaction's prior reads) using non-blocking tripwires, and that its performance depends on read/write tracking granularity and the abort rate, so keep read-write transactions short.

Use transactions as an abstraction that reduces a large class of concurrency problems and faults to a retryable abort, and select the isolation level by the anomaly you must prevent: read committed stops dirty reads and writes, snapshot isolation stops read skew, snapshot isolation or an explicit lock stops lost updates, only serializable isolation stops write skew, and index-range locks or serializable isolation stop write-skew phantoms.

Give stateful systems more care than stateless ones because a fault's effects can persist forever, recognize that strong-correctness tools (serializability and atomic commit) typically work only within a single datacenter and limit scale, and remember the end-to-end argument that strong database safety such as serializable transactions does not by itself prevent data loss or corruption from application bugs.

Distinguish system transactions (reliable but meaningless to the user) from business transactions (the user's logical unit of work, possibly spanning requests) and still aim to give business transactions ACID properties.

When long transactions are untenable, break the business transaction into a series of short system transactions and add application-level glue to preserve ACID across them (offline concurrency): commit atomically and durably in one final system transaction (a Unit of Work tracks the change set), treating isolation as the hard property to enforce.

Implement a business transaction as a single long system transaction only with modest concurrency needs — do it if you can get away with it since it avoids many problems — but expect it not to scale (the database becomes the bottleneck) and the later refactor to short transactions to be complex.

Execute all locking and standard domain business for a single request within one system transaction (for example by decorating the command with a transactional command) and mandatorily roll back that system transaction on a concurrency or any other exception, to keep conflicting changes out of the permanent record data.
Assume one business transaction runs within a single client session, because designing one business transaction across multiple sessions reliably causes confusion.

Reduce offline-locking complexity with a Coarse-Grained Lock (lock a group of related objects together) and an Implicit Lock (free developers from managing locks directly) to avoid hard-to-find bugs from a forgotten lock.

Implement Optimistic Offline Lock by bundling a version check into the UPDATE and DELETE statements and verifying that exactly one row was affected (a count of zero means the lock could not be obtained, so throw a concurrency exception), acquiring the locks within the same system transaction that commits the changes and, on detecting a violation, rolling back that system transaction as a step that must not be forgotten.

Choose among the three Pessimistic Offline Lock types (an exclusive write lock, fine when stale views are acceptable; an exclusive read lock, which severely restricts concurrency; and a read/write lock, which maximizes concurrency at the cost of complexity) to maximize concurrency, meet business needs, and minimize complexity, treating locking as a domain decision because a wrong locking strategy cannot be rescued by a correct technical implementation.

Use a single lock manager as the only code that touches locks, backed by exactly one lock table (a singleton in-memory hash table, or a database table when the application server is clustered), keeping the lock objects private to the manager.

Serialize access to the lock table, and with a database-backed lock table interact within a system transaction and use serializable isolation for read/write locks to avoid inconsistent reads (optionally isolating lock acquisition in its own serializable transaction to ease the performance cost), while reducing contention on the inherently serial lock table through coarser lock granularity such as a Coarse-Grained Lock.
Manage database locking for concurrency: tune lock granularity, let the optimizer choose then correct it, and pick an engine with flexible lock types.

Account for two-phase locking's costs: deadlocks occur easily and far more often than under read committed (the database aborts one transaction, which must retry), and throughput and latency are much worse than under weak isolation because of lock overhead and greatly reduced concurrency.
Treat the optimistic-versus-pessimistic choice as a product decision, not a deferrable technical detail: it shapes the whole user experience and requires input from the system's actual users.

Prefer process-per-request (or pooled process-per-request) over thread-per-request for request handling: it is equally scalable, more robust (a runaway thread can crash a whole process), and avoids threading headaches — worth the extra hardware, especially with a less experienced team.

If you must use thread-per-request, build an isolated zone: have each thread create fresh objects per request and never publish them to other threads; avoid static, class-based, or global variables and singletons (synchronize any unavoidable shared access), use a thread-scoped Registry for global memory, and pool only genuinely expensive objects like database connections.
Prefer stateless servers for resource efficiency: retaining no state between requests lets any pooled object serve any request and fits HTTP, so far fewer objects serve more (especially idle) users.

Recognize that much client interaction is inherently stateful (e.g., a shopping cart), so the real decision is where to keep session state — Client, Server, or Database Session State — treating it as transactional data that need only satisfy validation rules at business-transaction commit, distinct from disposable cached data, with isolation as its hardest problem.

Use Client Session State only when the session state is small (all of it travels over the wire every request) and always encrypt it, since unencrypted client-held state can be edited by a malicious user.
Isolate session data from other sessions, and with Database Session State work hard to keep session data isolated from the record data living in the same database.

Pick a session-state approach by data size and idle-user count, and account for failure and cancellation: Database Session State best survives client/server/network failure and suits many-idle retail systems; Server Session State suits data-heavy sessions; Client Session State makes abandoned sessions easy to forget; and non-client approaches need explicit timeout and cleanup.

Default to Server Session State (usually cheapest to build) backed by a remotely stored memento for crash survival; use Client Session State for session IDs and tiny data, and Database Session State only when you need failover and clustering and cannot store remote mementos.

Know that the simplest Server Session State holds session objects in memory keyed by session ID (assuming enough memory, no clustering, and that a server failure can simply abandon the session), and to avoid holding memory resources serialize it to a memento in as simple a form as possible: binary serialization is easy and compact but not human-readable and risks versioning breakage, while textual or XML needs more code.

Store serialized Server Session State either on the application server (file or local database, simple but poor for clustering and failover) or somewhere generally accessible such as a shared server or a database session table as a Serialized LOB (supporting clustering and failover at the cost of slower, cacheable activation), and when using a database provide a mechanism to expire old sessions (a cleanup daemon or rotating partitioned table segments) to avoid contention on the session table.

Understand Database Session State pulls the data a request needs from the database at the start and saves it back at the end (the client holds only the session-ID keys), which enables stateless server objects (allowing pooling and easy clustering) at the cost of reading and writing data each request (caching reduces the read cost), with clustering and failover usually more straightforward than Server Session State's.

Because session data is local to a session and must not affect the rest of the system until committed, separate pending session data from record data, either via a session-ID/pending field (invasive, since every application must filter it out) or via separate pending tables cloned from the real tables (less invasive but adding table-selection logic, and also letting you defer integrity and validation rules).

Provide a mechanism to clean up cancelled or abandoned session data using the session ID plus a timeout daemon driven by a table tracking each session's last interaction, and because rolling back updates to existing record data within a session is hard, consider the simple option of disallowing session cancellation and letting record-data updates become permanent at the end of each request, which often fits users' expectations.
Split session data — frequently used parts in the client's cookie, rarely used parts in a central store — to remove sticky sessions and radically improve load balancing.

When clustering, choose between session migration (sessions move server-to-server for better load balancing, good for long sessions) and server affinity (one server per session); beware affinity keyed on a proxy IP shared by many clients, which can overload one server.
Do not confuse session stickiness with load balancing: pinning a user to a server for locally stored session state creates a single point of failure.

Follow the First Law of Distributed Object Design: do not distribute your objects, because basing distribution on individual classes produces too many remote calls and a system awkward to build, deploy, and modify.

Be parsimonious with distribution boundaries: the genuinely unavoidable ones are client/server desktop, application-server/database (SQL is the remote interface), web-server/application-server, package/vendor, and rare genuine application-server splits.

At a distribution boundary keep fine-grained objects internal and expose a coarse-grained Remote Facade over them, paired with Data Transfer Objects (which reference only other DTOs and fundamental types) to move data across the wire in one block.

Use assembler objects to move data between domain objects and Data Transfer Objects (a plain data holder that collapses and flattens the domain object graph for transfer over the wire) so the facade stays thin, with the assembler writing the DTO from the domain model and the Remote Facade calling it.

On J2EE build with plain old Java objects and JDBC, keep a complex Domain Model entirely independent of the EJB container so you can write, run, and test it without container vagaries, and never give entity beans a remote interface (they need fine-grained interfaces, so keep them local).

Trade POJO versus stateless session bean for a Service Layer class: POJOs run and test without an EJB container, while session beans get container-managed distributed transactions but must be deployed to test.
In Enterprise Java use a session bean (stateful or stateless remote object) as a distributed facade and run plain Java objects inside the EJB container, so domain objects need not be entity beans.
Keep as much testing as possible in a single process by instantiating and testing the session-bean Remote Facade implementation directly, outside the EJB container, for a faster testing turnaround.

Avoid putting business logic in stored procedures despite their speed, because they cause vendor lock-in and lack good structuring mechanisms; move a specific method into one only as a targeted optimization when a clear, strong performance gain justifies it.
Separate business intelligence from transaction processing: keep stored procedures out of the database and move data between corporate and product systems asynchronously.

Separate Transaction Scripts as much as possible (at least into distinct subroutines, better into classes apart from presentation and data source) and never call presentation logic from a Transaction Script, to make the code easier to modify and test.

Organize Transaction Scripts either as several related scripts per subject-area class (best for most cases) or as one script per class using the Command pattern (only when you need to manipulate scripts as runtime objects, which is rare).

Keep Transaction Script in your toolkit however object-oriented you become: its simplicity adds very little performance or comprehension overhead and gets applications with only a little logic running much faster.
Instantiating a fresh object per Transaction Script can help with threading because it makes data easier to isolate.
Replace an in-memory script loop with a single SQL statement using an aggregate function when the calculation is simple enough.
In a Domain Model place behavior on the object that needs to know it, accepting that behavior spreads across many small collaborating objects, because this avoids duplication and reduces coupling.
Use the Strategy pattern in a Domain Model to provide well-contained plug points, adding a new algorithm by creating a subclass and overriding its method.

Let a Domain Model replace conditional logic with object structure: wiring objects together fixes the decision path, so similar conditionals factor into the object relationships and get reused across the system.
Use a Domain Model to hide the database both from the upper layers and from the people working within the model itself.

Understand Table Module as one class per table, view, or query with a single instance handling all rows (versus a Domain Model's object per row), and because it has no object identity, pass an identity reference (usually the primary key) into every operation.

Use Table Module when accessing tabular data via a Record Set with fairly straightforward access (especially when other parts share a table-oriented structure such as .NET Record Sets), but prefer a Domain Model for complex domain logic because Table Module lacks direct instance relationships and strong polymorphism.

Use Identity Field when mapping in-memory objects to database rows (typically with a Domain Model or Row Data Gateway); it is not needed for Transaction Script, Table Module, or Table Data Gateway, while small value objects with no own table are better handled by Embedded Value and a complex unqueried object graph by Serialized LOB.

Identify Service Layer operations from the use-case model and the user-interface design, since the UI is typically the first and most significant client, and expect an almost one-to-one correspondence between CRUD use cases and Service Layer operations.

Use a Service Layer when business logic has more than one kind of client and use-case responses span multiple transactional resources, designing it in from the start once you foresee a second client or resource; skip it when there is a single client with no multi-resource responses and let Page Controllers manage transactions.

Distinguish Service Layer (which factors responsibility to avoid duplication and promote reuse and transcends any particular technology) from Session Facade (which exists to avoid the performance penalty of too many remote invocations on entity beans).
Avoid embedding database-access code in in-memory objects that also carry business logic, because it increases complexity and slows tests by making them hit the database.

Generate the tedious database-access code of Row Data Gateways automatically from a Metadata Mapping at build time, and combine auto-generated Row Data Gateways with hand-written Data Mappers when that division of labor fits.
For a very simple domain, build the Data Transfer Objects directly from a Table Data Gateway rather than introducing a full Domain Model.

When Transaction Script plus Row Data Gateway shows business logic repeated across scripts, move that logic into the Row Data Gateway, gradually turning it into an Active Record and reducing duplication.

Give mappers access to domain-object fields without exposing persistence-only setters and getters and never by making fields public: package mappers close to the domain objects, use reflection (negligible against SQL time), or status-guarded methods named so they are not mistaken for regular accessors.

When loading objects, prefer a rich constructor that supplies all mandatory data (it yields a well-formed object from the start and can enforce immutability) over creating an empty object and then populating it.

Break cyclic references during load by creating a blank object with a no-arg constructor and inserting it into the Identity Map immediately, so an in-progress cycle returns the partially built object instead of recursing.

Store field-to-column mapping either as explicit code (one mapper class per domain object, the simplest and often best approach) or as Metadata Mapping (data in a class or file that absorbs mapping variation via code generation or reflection without extra source code).

Implement Metadata Mapping as either code generation (a program turns metadata into mapper source built before compilation, requiring recompile and redeploy) or reflective programming (reading field and method names from metadata and invoking them dynamically, changeable even at runtime without recompiling); either way mapping changes are rare because they imply database or code changes.

Hold mapping metadata in a separate file (XML is popular, giving hierarchic structure without a custom parser), directly in source code (avoids parsing but is harder to edit), or in the database itself (keeping the mapping co-located with the data and its schema changes).
Do not build a full-featured database-mapping layer yourself; it is complex, so for most cases buy one rather than build one.

Use a Repository to mediate between domain and data-mapping layers through a collection-like interface: clients build query specifications declaratively and submit them for satisfaction, which replaces specialized finder methods so client code works purely in objects and never thinks in SQL.

Do not write to the database on every object-model change, because it produces many small slow database calls and forces a transaction to stay open for the whole interaction, which is impractical when a business transaction spans multiple requests.

Register objects with a Unit of Work by caller registration (flexible but error-prone, since a forgotten call drops the change) or object registration (load registers clean, setters register dirty, removing the caller burden but still needing registration calls in the right places), and lean on code generation, aspect-oriented programming, or bytecode post-processing to keep that registration code separate from domain code.

Consider unit-of-work-controller variants where the Unit of Work handles all reads and copies each object at read time to compare at commit (avoiding registration calls and enabling selective field update at commit cost), and for transient objects provide a non-registering constructor or, better, a Special Case Unit of Work whose commit does nothing.
Let objects find their current Unit of Work through a thread-scoped Registry (or by passing it in), and never allow more than one thread to access a single Unit of Work.

Use the Unit of Work as the natural point for batch updates (sending multiple SQL commands in one remote call, checking it does not interfere with statement precompilation), and remember it works with any transactional resource, not just databases.

Prefer Unit of Work for keeping all change-tracking in one place and as a firm platform for offline concurrency locks, since the alternatives are weaker: explicit save-on-change causes too many calls, variable tracking becomes unmanageable in a Domain Model, and per-object dirty flags only help when dirty objects are easy to find.
Know Lazy Load's four implementations: lazy initialization, virtual proxy, value holder, and ghost.

Make Lazy Load a candidate for aspect-oriented programming or bytecode post-processing so the strategy can vary separately and domain developers are freed from lazy-loading concerns, and because different use cases need different laziness, use separate mappers (eager and lazy) or a strategy object, but in practice only two degrees (a full load and enough for list identification) are worth the complexity.

Implement lazy initialization by checking each field access for null and loading on demand, which requires the field to be self-encapsulated and fails when null is a legal value (use a different not-loaded marker or a Special Case); because it forces a dependency on the database it suits Active Record, Table Data Gateway, and Row Data Gateway, while with Data Mapper you add a virtual proxy for the needed indirection.

Do not Lazy Load a field stored in the same row as the rest of the object (there is no extra cost to fetch it); only consider Lazy Load when accessing the field requires an extra database call and the data is not used when the main object is, and since it adds complexity, avoid it unless you actively expect to need it.

Split mapper behavior into find (locating the right database row) and load (populating the domain object from that row), putting the default behavior for simple integral keys in a mapper Layer Supertype via a template method and overriding hook methods only for more complex keys.

Use a virtual proxy that mimics the real object and loads it on first method call, but guard against identity problems (multiple proxies holding different identities) by overriding the equality method and comparing with it; these problems disappear when proxies wrap only collection classes, which are Value Objects whose identity does not matter.

Use a value holder that loads its object on first access only with care: the owning class must know the value holder is present and you lose strong-typing explicitness, so avoid identity problems by never passing the value holder beyond its owning class.

Use a ghost (the real object in a partial state, initially just its ID, that loads full state on first field access) and put it into the Identity Map immediately to maintain identity and avoid cyclic-reference problems; a ghost or virtual proxy may preload quick, commonly used data as a light object.
Expect inheritance to complicate Lazy Load, because with ghosts (and with virtual proxies in statically typed languages) you may not know which subtype to create without loading the object properly.

Beware ripple loading: a collection filled with Lazy Loads and iterated one at a time causes one database call per object and can cripple performance, so make the collection itself a single Lazy Load that loads all its contents at once, except for very large collections where you need a Value List Handler.

Distrust meaningful keys such as a Social Security number and usually choose meaningless keys, because keys must be unique and immutable but human error makes meaningful keys neither; tolerate meaningful keys only for small or very stable cases.

Prefer simple single-field keys for the uniformity of one key-manipulation code path; use compound keys when one table makes sense only in another's context (such as order number plus line-item sequence), but guard their uniqueness and immutability because compound keys carry meaning.

Choose a key type with fast equality (the most common key operation) and easy next-key generation (a long integer is often best) and avoid dates or times in keys (meaningful, with portability and precision-sync problems); database-unique keys are often easier than table-unique keys and allow a single Identity Map, and with Class Table or Concrete Table Inheritance use keys unique across the inheritance hierarchy.

Choose a key-generation source aware of its constraints: a database auto-increment field usually does not reveal the key before commit, so you generally cannot use it where you must insert connected objects (such as an order and its line items needing the order's key as a foreign key), whereas a database counter or sequence is ideal (runs in a separate transaction, returns multiple keys at once) but is nonstandard and not in every database.
Represent a compound key as a dedicated key class whose essential behavior is equality, and centralize key handling in a Layer Supertype with default behavior extended for exceptional cases.
Know the three ways to obtain a new key: let the database auto-generate it, use a GUID, or generate your own.

Weigh GUID and home-grown key schemes: a GUID is globally unique and safe but its large string is hard to read and may hurt index performance, while the SQL max-plus-one table scan read-locks the whole table, works only when inserts are rare, and needs full transaction isolation to avoid two transactions getting the same ID.

Prefer a separate key table (name plus next-available value) for roll-your-own keys: fetch many keys at once to cut database calls and contention, and access the key table in its own short transaction so the lock is not held for the whole business transaction, accepting only that a rolled-back insert wastes a cheap key.

Generally acquire the lock before loading the data so you are guaranteed the latest version, and lock the ID or primary key rather than the object (which lets you lock before loading); release locks when the business transaction completes and do not release early without a specific reason such as a serious liveness problem.
Separate new-key-generation code into its own class so it is easy to replace with a Service Stub for testing.
Extract the parts of a compound key through named helper methods rather than literal numeric indices, because literal positional indices into a key are a code smell that obscures intent.
Insert an empty object directly into the Identity Map to remove the special handling otherwise needed when an associated object is not yet registered during loads.
Always check the Identity Map on load so different versions of the same object are not loaded within one business transaction, which would cause undefined behavior and corrupt version checks.

Recognize the genuine tension over where to place code that maps a SQL result into a referenced object: putting it on the referenced object's own mapper keeps it with the class that usually loads it, while keeping it with the query reflects that the load logic is tightly coupled to the SQL.
Turn a complicated method into a method object that holds intermediate state in fields instead of passing it through parameters: create it, run it once, and discard it.

Keep a result-set loader generic and independent of specific domain classes by passing in a small callback interface (such as an Adder) that the caller implements, and distinguish a load method (which does whatever is needed and may advance the cursor) from a loadRow method (which loads a row without moving the result-set cursor).
Treat generated mapping code as never hand-edited: integrate generation fully into the build and do not keep the generated classes in source control.
Default to code generation over reflection because generated mapping code is more explicit and easier to debug, especially for less sophisticated developers.

Accept reflection for database mapping even though reflection is generally worth avoiding, because here you are reading field and method names from a file and its overhead is usually small relative to the SQL call (measure in your environment), and metadata access and parsing performance is mostly negligible since code generation parses at build time and reflection parses once at startup then caches.
Evolve metadata complexity as your needs grow rather than building a fully general mapping scheme up front, because it is not hard to add new capabilities to metadata-driven software.

Handle special cases that would over-complicate a simple metadata scheme by overriding the generic code with handwritten subclasses (isolating a single overridable method per special case), and reduce hand-coding by writing a good Layer Supertype for the common behavior so only a few hook routines remain, which Metadata Mapping can then reduce further.

Weigh that Metadata Mapping can interfere with code refactoring (automated tools cannot find field names hidden in a mapping file, so renaming a private field can silently break the application, with no warning under reflection) against its making database refactoring easier because the metadata states the schema interface.

Use a Query Object to express a query in the language of domain objects and fields rather than table structure (holding the target class and criteria that map to where-clause predicates and translating itself into SQL), and build complex criteria as polymorphic subclasses so each criterion knows how to generate its own SQL fragment.
Remember that a Repository's apparent in-memory collection may map to a huge table, so operations like all() over a catalog of hundreds of thousands of rows are unwise.

Understand that under the covers a Repository combines Metadata Mapping with a Query Object to generate SQL automatically from the criteria, and that some objects (such as immutable ones) can stay in memory and never be queried for again once loaded.

Exploit that a Repository's object source need not be a relational database: because the data-mapping component can be swapped via strategy objects, Repository suits multiple schemas or sources and lets unit-test suites run entirely in memory by backing it with an in-memory store, simplifying fixtures since you just construct objects and add them to a collection.
Use model objects directly as view helpers only when the helper would be a dumb forwarder, and keep any servlet-dependent code in a separate helper class rather than in the model.

Keep a Template View ideally playing only the view in Model View Controller, with any controller or model responsibility living in the helper rather than the page, and catch exceptions in the helper class because an exception reaching the web container can yield odd half-rendered output instead of a redirect.

When a server page acts as the request handler, delegate the controller function to a helper class (scriptlet code is bad design); let a handler-as-default-view revert control to itself unless it forwards elsewhere, and replace a clumsy helper-initialization scriptlet with a custom tag that creates, registers, and initializes the helper.

Use a Front Controller to route all requests through a single handler that instantiates the appropriate command (named, for example, by a URL parameter), initializes it, and runs its process method with commands sharing init/forward through a superclass, and use a Special Case such as an UnknownCommand for unrecognized requests to avoid extra error-checking code.

Compose a dynamic page like a static page with embedded markers that resolve into calls gathering the dynamic information (Template View) rather than concatenating HTML strings in code, embedding markers as HTML-like tags (best for WYSIWYG and XML tools), special text markers (easier syntax but editors may mangle them), or your own custom tags.

Treat general-purpose conditional tags such as a generic IF as a bad smell because they turn templates into a programming language: move the condition into the helper (returning an empty string when false) or use a focused tag driven by a single Boolean helper property, and require any in-page condition to rest on a single Boolean property of the helper.
Choose how template processing happens: compile the page after creation, compile it on first request, or interpret it on each request, avoiding the last when interpretation is slow.

Run an XSLT Transform View by feeding it XML, ideally the natural return type of the domain logic and otherwise produced via a self-serializing Data Transfer Object or a Transaction Script that returns XML directly, passing a DOM rather than a string unless a string form is needed to cross a communication line.

Choose between Transform View and Template View mostly by the team's preferred environment and tool availability (HTML editors are more mature than XSLT tools and XSLT's functional style and XML syntax are awkward to master), while valuing XSLT's portability to almost any web platform, since the same XSLT can transform XML produced from J2EE or .NET.

Use Transform View to avoid two of Template View's biggest problems (it is easier to keep focused only on rendering and easy to run and capture for testing without a web server), but because it transforms directly to HTML a site-wide appearance change can force changes across many transforms, so reduce that with common transforms such as XSLT includes or use a Two Step View when you need easy global changes or multiple appearances for the same data.

Weigh an object-based (non-XSLT) Two Step View, which constrains site-layout uniformity less and lets a page author slip in individual HTML more easily, but whose same openness permits inappropriate use, so the team must weigh that flexibility against the way constraints prevent mistakes.

Use an Application Controller to centralize screen-navigation and application-flow logic (such as wizard-style ordered or conditional screens), removing the duplication that arises when multiple input controllers each must know what to do, since it decides which domain logic to run and which view to display and typically holds two collections of references (domain commands and views, stored as Commands, function references, or reflectively invoked strings).

Prefer an Application Controller with no links to the UI machinery so you can test it independently of the UI and reuse it across presentations (treating it as an intermediate layer between presentation and domain), splitting an application into multiple Application Controllers by broad UI areas while a simple application needs only one.

Let the same Application Controller serve multiple presentations (web, rich client, PDA) but do not be too eager, because different UIs often need different screen flow for usability, so reusing one may cut development effort at the cost of a more awkward UI.

Model a user interface as a state machine (events trigger different responses depending on state) and let an Application Controller represent that control flow as metadata, set up either in code or in a separate configuration file.

Design every interface to handle undesired circumstances and tell actors whether their interaction succeeded, treating the specification of exceptions, status codes, and error events as part of the interface, and gracefully handle invalid input, wrong-state requests, hardware/software failure, and misconfiguration.

Offer remote method variants that move data either as a Data Transfer Object or as an XML string so the client can choose by its nature and connection, accepting that this multiplies the number of methods on the facade.
Make a distributed facade a long list of very short methods with very little logic, each merely delegating to another object, because the facade is only a packaging mechanism.
When updating the domain from a Data Transfer Object, decide per case whether to update the existing domain object or replace it with a new one, based on whether other objects reference it.

Prefer map-based Data Transfer Object serialization over native binary serialization, because binary requires the DTO classes on both sides of the wire to stay in sync (a server-side change without a matching client change causes transfer errors) whereas a map-based form is more tolerant, since added server fields are simply ignored by older clients.

In Java make free binary serialization via a marker interface the first choice for a Data Transfer Object (with text-based serialization such as XML often necessary), and avoid tedious hand-written serialization by using a reflective routine on a Layer Supertype, which handles most cases with extra code only for primitives.

Set version and modification fields in the mapper rather than through a constructor, so version-storage responsibility is not pushed down into each concrete mapper and domain object, which would weaken the Implicit Lock.
Have the Data Mapper insert the shared version before inserting the corresponding domain objects and increment it before updating or deleting an object.

When a lock cannot be acquired, abort immediately by throwing an exception rather than waiting, which avoids deadlock and timeout complexity, and acquire contentious locks as early as possible, ideally all before the user begins work.

Manage lock timeouts for lost sessions (such as crashed web clients) by preferring the application server's session-timeout mechanism to release locks when the HTTP session invalidates, or by timestamping each lock and treating old ones as invalid.

Implement a database lock manager as your own application lock table (not the database's internal locking), where acquiring a lock inserts a row and releasing deletes it, using a system-wide-unique long primary key as the lockable ID and the HTTP session ID as the owner, and have acquireLock first verify the owner does not already hold the lock (session code commonly re-acquires) while recognizing these repetitive lock-table reads add contention, so consider caching owned locks at the session level.

Give the layers beneath the web tier their own application session (distinct from the HTTP session) that stores an ID, user, and Identity Map and is bound to the executing thread via thread-local storage so it can be found, releasing any locks held by a prior application session when starting a new business transaction and registering a listener to release an application session's locks when its HTTP session expires.

If you must use Pessimistic Offline Lock, also consider a long transaction instead (sometimes no more damaging and easier to program, so load-test first), and do not use offline locking at all when business transactions fit within a single system transaction, where built-in mechanisms such as SELECT FOR UPDATE or entity-EJB locking suffice, remembering that all offline-locking techniques depend on having a real transaction monitor.
Use a disconnected Record Set as a Unit of Work: modify it and return it to the data source to commit, with Optimistic Offline Lock checking for conflicts before writing.

Handle shared-version deletion carefully: for an aggregate delete the version right after deleting the aggregate root, otherwise consider reference counting, which complicates the version possibly enough to make it a full domain object.

Do not assume stateless session beans are always better than stateful ones for performance: load-test first, because the difference appears only under heavy load, and if the advantage is insignificant and stateful beans are easier, use them.

If pending tables are read only by the objects handling a session, do not tabularize the data; use a Serialized LOB instead (which crosses into Server Session State), and better still, where feasible, design so all data is record data to avoid pending-data hassles entirely.

Use a Mapper as an insulating layer that controls two subsystems' communication without either being aware of it (driven by a third subsystem or by observing events in one), but because a Gateway is simpler to write and use and far more common, reserve a Mapper for when neither subsystem may depend on the interaction, typically a complicated and independent interaction such as a database (Data Mapper).

Use a Layer Supertype (a superclass for all objects in a layer, such as a Domain Object superclass) to hold common features like Identity Field handling without duplication, and use more than one Layer Supertype when a layer has more than one kind of object.

Recognize that an abstract class can serve as a good interface because it can carry common but optional implementation behavior, and bind a Separated Interface's implementation through a separate factory (itself behind a Separated Interface) with a Plugin to defer the choice to configuration time, or more simply let a startup package that knows both interface and implementation wire things up.

Do not write a separate interface for every class, which is excessive for application development; use one only to break a dependency or to allow multiple independent implementations, since separating them later is a simple refactoring you can delay.

Treat the interface as a fundamental two-way abstraction (what an element provides and requires) that has outsized impact on modifiability, usability, testability, performance, and integrability, recognizing every element has interfaces and a single interface may serve multiple actors.

Use a Registry as a well-known, apparently global object to find common objects and services when you lack an appropriate object to navigate from, designing its interface separately from its implementation and preferring a static-method interface that is easy to find anywhere and can encapsulate delegation.

Represent monetary values with a dedicated Money class holding an amount and a currency, because money is not a first-class type and naive handling causes currency-mixing errors and pennies lost to rounding, storing the amount as an integral or fixed-decimal type and absolutely avoiding floating point, which reintroduces those rounding errors.

Use distinct types for whole-unit and fractional-unit money because they behave differently under arithmetic (making clear which you are working with), and because Money is a Value Object override its equality and hash-code operations to be based on currency and amount.

Make money arithmetic currency- and rounding-aware: treat adding monies of different currencies as an error or use a money bag holding multiple currencies, distribute a sum with an allocator that distributes by ratios and scatters the remainder pennies (distinguishing proportional charge by multiplication from allocation by an allocator), and convert currency through a convertor object that encapsulates the conversion algorithm rather than a bare exchange-rate multiplication.

Encapsulate currency-aware printing and parsing inside Money to ease display and input (leveraging the platform's globalization number formatters) and store it via Embedded Value (a currency per money), except that for a single-currency account you can store the currency on the account and pull it during mapping to avoid repeating it on every entry.

Use a Money type for essentially all numeric calculation in object-oriented environments to encapsulate rounding and ease multi-currency work (the common performance objection rarely matters and the encapsulation makes tuning easier), and always question accessors on a Value Object because there is almost always a way that does not break encapsulation, with database mapping via Embedded Value being a rare unavoidable exception.

Recognize that enterprise systems often depend on problematic third-party services (credit scoring, tax, pricing) whose unpredictability slows development and can stop tests from running, and replace such a service during testing with a Service Stub that runs locally, fast, and in memory.

When a dynamic Service Stub needs test-setup methods not on the Gateway interface, add those methods to the Gateway and make the real-service implementation throw assertion failures if they are called, and use a Service Stub whenever dependence on a particular service hinders development and testing (Extreme Programming practitioners call this a Mock Object).

Use a Record Set (an in-memory tabular structure that looks like a query result yet can be manipulated by other code, usually provided by the platform such as an ADO.NET data set or JDBC row set) to get both easy relational display and a home for business logic that data-aware UI tools otherwise force into stored procedures or UI code, and disconnect it from the data source so you can pass it across a network and serialize it as a Data Transfer Object.

Prefer an explicit, typed interface over an implicit one for Record Sets, because implicit interfaces (generic field-name access or passing data in dictionaries) hide which fields exist and lose type information in statically typed languages; use strongly typed data sets (as in ADO.NET) or code generation for explicit Record Sets.
Default to simplicity: avoid overengineering, simplify scope/design/implementation, and reuse proven solutions before building your own.
Focus on the nature of the solution, not the implementation language: solutions scale, languages do not.
