Make reducing complexity a primary design goal because complexity raises the risk of bugs when changing the system, and remove accidental complexity (that which arises only from the implementation, not the problem) chiefly through good, reusable abstractions that hide implementation detail.
Design scale in early with the D-I-D process — design for 20x, implement for 3x, deploy for ~1.5x — so capacity arrives just in time.
Trim work the browser must do: reduce DNS lookups and page objects, balanced against the browser's per-domain connection cap, and verify by testing.
Standardize routing and switching gear on one vendor; use best-of-breed for non-routing devices like firewalls and load balancers.

Build platform standards that split IT into a standardized non-differentiating lower layer (best drawn from slow-changing networking and hardware) and an in-house upper layer for differentiation, distinguished from plain layering by self-service access and a broad center of gravity.
Scale out on commodity hardware, not up on big high-end systems, because scaling up follows a power-law cost curve and eventually hits a ceiling.
Own your scalability: scale your own system rather than relying on vendor/proprietary features, keeping destiny, simplicity, and total cost in your control.
Scale out, not up: prefer horizontal scaling by adding more of the same commodity hardware, and reserve vertical scaling for problems with no horizontally-scalable solution.
Account for scaling down as well as up: keep the application able to run on a smaller footprint so falling demand can cut operating cost.
Weigh every scaling decision as a cost-benefit trade-off across capital, complexity, maintenance, and time, remembering the best technical option is not always the right business one.
Design for three or more live data centers and leverage the cloud for spiky demand, rather than a two-site hot/cold pair.
Use the right storage tool for the data: reserve RDBMS for ACID/relationship needs and choose file systems or NoSQL otherwise, recognizing relationships trade flexibility against scale.
Do not use an RDBMS when ACID is not needed; 'too slow' usually means the wrong tool, so choose data structures and a platform that answer your exact questions cheaply.

Consider a nonrelational (NoSQL) store when you need greater scalability or write throughput than relational databases easily provide, specialized query operations, or schema flexibility, and expect polyglot persistence in which relational and nonrelational stores coexist because the best technology differs per use case.

Rely on document storage locality only when the application needs large parts of a document at once, and keep documents fairly small while avoiding writes that grow them, because the database loads and rewrites the whole document; note that grouping related data for locality is not unique to documents and is also offered by relational systems like Spanner, Oracle clusters, and Bigtable column families.
Treat firewalls as a risk-versus-cost decision: firewall high-value data (PII/PCI) and leave low-value static content unfirewalled.
Actively use log files — aggregate out-of-band, monitor with automated tools, and assign owners to fix what they reveal — while logging asynchronously to limit cost.
Deliver all logs reliably in real-time over a publish/subscribe substrate with reliable IP multicast, and separate logging roles (publish, journal, analyze) so each scales independently.
Turn the log stream into real-time business-level monitors and build your own cluster tooling from it; correlate technical and business metrics to spot a forming problem.

Treat a log as a bounded circular disk buffer whose old segments are eventually discarded, so monitor how far each consumer lags the head of the log and alert before it falls behind the retained buffer and misses messages, and exploit that consuming is a read-only operation advancing only the consumer's offset to replay old messages by resetting the offset, which makes log-based messaging behave like a repeatable batch process for experimentation and recovery.
Do not duplicate work: never read-after-write to validate, act on returned error codes, and cache data you will reuse soon.
Avoid redirects where possible; when required, use server-config redirects with the correct HTTP 3xx status rather than HTML or code.
Relax temporal constraints and embrace eventual consistency (BASE), because CAP makes strong consistency expensive to scale.
Cache in depth — CDN, page cache, application cache, object cache — using HTTP headers (not meta tags) and monitoring hit ratios.
The key to caching is understanding your data: how often it changes and where it is used.
Build a learning organization: learn from customers via fast launches and A/B testing, and from operations via blameless postmortems on every incident.
Use QA to lower cost and raise throughput and defect detection, not to add quality, since you cannot test quality into a system.
Always be able to roll back: keep database changes additive, script and load-test rollback, avoid in-release semantic data changes, and add a feature-flag (wire-on/wire-off) framework.
Design the data model up front, because relationships dictate how the database can be split and fixing the model later can cost ~100x.
Avoid lock-and-wait database patterns: do not use multiphase commits, and minimize SELECT ... FOR UPDATE cursors.

Prevent the lost-update problem (two concurrent read-modify-write cycles where the later clobbers the earlier) by preferring built-in atomic write operations such as an in-database increment when the change can be expressed that way, and otherwise by explicit locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE, taking care because it is easy to forget a needed lock.
Never use SELECT * or unnamed INSERT; name columns explicitly to avoid breakage, wasted transfer, and loss of rollback.
Design fault-isolative swimlanes along Y/Z boundaries: share nothing, allow no synchronous cross-swimlane calls, limit async ones, and keep swimlanes on physical boundaries.
Eliminate single points of failure and avoid components in series: strive for active/active and add parallel redundancy, especially at the database and network layers.
Use triple modular redundancy (three components plus voting) as a cost/availability sweet spot for the voting tactic, since the chance of two or more simultaneous failures is vanishingly small.
Provide graceful failure with wire-on/wire-off frameworks for risky or shared services, justified when implementation cost is below the risk-weighted cost of failure.
Strive for statelessness; if state is required, push it to the browser, and otherwise use a distributed cache without affinity or replication.

Push stable, shared page content out to the web server with two-tier execution so neither the database nor a remote cache is touched, since whole-page transparent caching fails when only part of a page is cacheable.
Match storage cost to data value with RFM analysis and tiered storage, purging or archiving low-value data, because storage is never free.
Design applications to be monitored, driving monitoring from business metrics first ('Is there a problem?'), then 'Where', then 'What'.
Be competent in every component you deploy — build-vs-buy is not an excuse for incompetence — because to the customer every problem is yours.
Prioritize scalability work by risk reduction minus cost (R - C = P), measuring availability by revenue impact, and codify chosen rules as enforced architectural principles.
Treat scalability and performance as distinct properties: a fast component can still fail to scale, and a single slow or non-scaling component can cap or capsize the whole architecture.
Build architectures from autonomous, independently scalable components so a demand spike stresses only one or two; component architectures scale better than monoliths.
A service scales when it collects information outside the critical path, so it can run everywhere without loading other components; that, not per-box throughput, is real scalability.

Do not call a system scalable or unscalable in the abstract; instead describe its current load with a small set of architecture-appropriate load parameters and frame scalability as concrete questions about how to cope as those parameters grow.
Expect sublinear horizontal scaling: doubling machines does not double capacity and per-server utilization falls, so plan capacity at about 70% per server on clusters of three or more nodes.
Prefer commodity, current- or prior-generation hardware for return on investment over the fastest, biggest hardware.
Use version control for everything as the baseline failure-avoidance practice: require atomic commits, run it on every platform you operate, and leverage it for deployment, not just development.
Keep production configuration under version control so non-bare-metal failures are tracked and recoverable; understanding how configuration changed over time beats a point-in-time restore.
Require a complete push plan for every production change: a forward plan, a tested rollback, a bare-metal restore, and a successful test of the forward and rollback plans.
Recognize and resist uncontrolled change (feature creep, milestone hopping, sloppy version control, premature implementation) with disciplined tools and process.
Adopt unit testing to catch breakage from rapid change, testing the whole system for real confidence, while remembering that testing only proves expected output for the inputs you supply.

Apply safety detection and substitution tactics: substitute hardware protection (watchdogs, monitors, interlocks) for simple dangerous software functions, use predictive models with condition monitoring for early warning, use timeouts to catch late and omission failures, and use comparison of replicated outputs to detect and, with three or more replicas, localize an unsafe state.

Master the five aspects of a mission-critical environment — high availability, monitoring, software management, avoiding overcomplication, and optimization — and never entrust the architecture to a single person.
Run three environments — development, staging, and production — and make staging as close to production as possible (ideally identical down to versions); production should stay quiet.
Decide infrastructure investment by cost-benefit: a full development and staging environment is not always worth it, but the calculus is business-specific.
Apply emergency releases (security exploits or crippling bugs) with extreme haste but as safely as possible.
Monitor both bottom-up (systems) and top-down (business) metrics, because bottom-up alone is incomplete and what ultimately matters is that the business is running.
Keep monitoring in lock-step with architecture, application, and business changes, and do not blindly trust an HA solution — stale monitoring creates a dangerous false sense of security.

Require capable-monitoring features: automatic escalation, a service-dependency graph that suppresses downstream alert storms, maintenance windows and event acknowledgment instead of disabling monitors, and scheduling by cost and volatility.

Specify availability requirements as scenarios whose stimulus is a fault and whose response options include detect, log, notify, recover, mask, contain, disable the source, or degrade, with measures such as availability percentage, time to detect, and time to repair; exclude scheduled downtime per the SLA.
Monitor a distributed service by exercising it on a representative task and checking the result, not by checking a single daemon's health.
Treat high availability and load balancing as orthogonal — HA is resilience to failure, LB is about scale — and define which (or both) a system needs before implementing.
Eliminate single points of failure, including the load balancer itself (deploy two with an HA solution); hardware needed for routine load is not redundant, and selling points are not buying points.

Prefer peer-based high availability — where the cluster owns the services and IP addresses and each node negotiates a subset — over idle hot-standby pairs and dedicated HA hardware as you scale horizontally or across sites.

For peer-based HA with multiple active machines, each node must serve authoritatively and tolerate concurrent use; refresh neighbors' ARP caches with gratuitous ARP on IP failover, and test HA by actually killing a node.
Understand fault-tolerance terms (1-fault-tolerant vs N-1) and that no enterprise-ready, horizontally scalable, N-1-fault-tolerant database exists — engineer around it.

Distinguish a fault (one component deviating from spec) from a failure (the whole system ceasing to serve users), and design fault-tolerance mechanisms that stop faults from escalating into failures rather than trying to eliminate faults, since fault probability cannot be reduced to zero.

Expect hardware faults to be routine at scale and treat component redundancy as a partial measure that lowers but cannot eliminate single-machine failure; as machine counts grow, favor software fault-tolerance that survives the loss of whole machines and enables zero-downtime rolling upgrades.
Base load balancing on effective utilization of available resources, not system load average, which is too stale for short web requests.

Let requirements, not convenience, dictate the load-balancing solution: if a web switch or IPVS cannot meet a functional need it is eliminated, and application-layer balancers buy features (SSL-content and business-rule routing) at a performance cost.

Choose load-balancing algorithms for their trade-offs and make parallel balancers cooperate, since uncooperative balancers double their intended effect and a random distribution can beat the smartest uncooperative algorithm.

Plan SSL/IP consumption deliberately: a single IP serves at most one SSL common name, SSL blocks name-based virtual hosting, and workarounds (non-default ports, delegate namespaces) carry firewall and user-trust costs.
Use a reverse-proxy cache to offload origins: serve previously seen content from cache and absorb slow-client TCP handling so expensive application servers move to the next job.
Optimize for the user's network proximity, not geography, and combine Anycast DNS (using connectionless UDP) with unique per-node IPs to route clients to the nearest cluster — Anycast breaks TCP.
Align static- and dynamic-content distribution mechanisms to reduce human error, and keep dynamic code consistent across all nodes.
Apply computational reuse and caching where re-finding a result is cheaper than recomputing it, remembering this buys performance, not scalability (but low performance is fatal).
A computer cache is only an optimization — a miss costs only time — so design cacheable data to carry an explicit TTL and treat the cache as purgeable at will.

Choose cache semantics deliberately: TTL caching is easy and approximate, explicit invalidation is complex and correct; for high read-to-write data you control, prefer caching indefinitely and invalidating on change.
Cache per-user data in the user's own cookie — a wildly scalable, user-centric cache — and secure it with encryption for confidentiality plus a digest for integrity.
Replication is hard because of ACID and you cannot get both availability and performance from multimaster replication; pick the technique that matches the need rather than assuming multimaster.
Survive network partitions in multimaster replication with a quorum algorithm (at most one quorum at any time), tunable to business priorities; EVS gives ordered messaging without 2PC's cost.
For horizontal read scaling, use master-slave replication (the only approach that scales horizontally): writes at the master, read-only queries on slaves.

Combine vertical scale-up and horizontal scale-out (shared-nothing) pragmatically rather than committing to one extreme, choose elastic scaling for highly unpredictable load but manual scaling for simplicity and fewer surprises, and keep a stateful data system on a single node until scaling cost or high-availability needs force distribution.

Choose operation vs changeset replication by your DML profile (changeset for expensive-small changes and LANs, operation for cheap-large changes and WANs); massive or expensive-tiny-result queries should be rare in OLTP.
Replay replication by transaction ID, not timestamp, because in databases 'since' means since-commit; track each node's processed transactions.

Limit the number of distinct products and use the same product for the same job unless the new demand genuinely differs; for a horizontally scaled read tier, use cheaper replicas around the proven core and avoid changing what works.
Avoid the inadequate classic logging approaches: batch aggregation loses logs and rewrites history, naive Syslog over UDP is unreliable, and passive sniffing drops logs silently and cannot read SSL.
Set up metric collection and visualization before problems occur, define your metrics precisely, and graph the right breakdown so anomalies are obvious.
Centralize logging to one audit portal that remains accessible even when a misbehaving machine is unreachable.
Never make a non-essential side task synchronous with serving a request; process derived data passively from the free log stream so a surge only causes a small lag.
Profile rather than guess when performance is surprising, test against production-representative data after warm-up, and test in the real deployment shape for confidence.
Know your tools: pick features by principle, weigh the cost of features you do not need, match the delivery/consistency guarantee to the need, and keep configuration identical across nodes.
Apply trade-off analysis as a repeatable, documented process, attending to the method used to reach the decision and not only the final answer.

Build trade-off analysis as a core architect skill and apply the three-step method: find what parts are entangled, analyze how they are coupled, then assess trade-offs by determining the impact of change on interdependent systems.
Evaluate any architecture style against the constraints of its era and context, recognizing that shifts in capability (such as operationally free infrastructure) drive which styles become dominant.

Apply the same granularity-versus-interdependency trade-off reasoning at every level — software, business structure, and centralization — recognizing architecture as fractal, and equip enterprise-scale architects to navigate organizational and political legacy.
Treat data as a first-class, long-lived architectural concern: design explicitly for who may read and write data and for separating operational (OLTP) from analytical data.

Distinguish OLTP from OLAP because they call for different engines: OLTP looks up a few records by key with interactive low-latency writes while OLAP scans many records reading few columns to compute aggregates, and although SQL serves both, analytics is run on a separate data warehouse rather than on the transaction-processing system.

Do not run ad hoc analytic queries directly on guarded OLTP databases, since such queries harm concurrent transactions; instead use a separate read-only data warehouse loaded by ETL and optimized for analytic access patterns, because OLTP indexing algorithms serve analytic queries poorly.

Recognize that storage engines split into OLTP-optimized engines (user-facing, fetching a few records by key, bottlenecked on disk seek time) and analytics-optimized engines (scanning many records, bottlenecked on disk bandwidth, favoring column storage), that OLTP engines follow either the log-structured (append-only) or update-in-place (B-tree) school, and that understanding these internals helps you choose the right tool and reason about tuning.

Consider actual serial execution (one transaction at a time on a single thread, serializable by definition) when the active dataset fits in memory and OLTP transactions are short, submitting each transaction ahead of time as a stored procedure to avoid interactive network round-trips and keeping transactions short, using modern stored procedures written in general-purpose languages.
Expect tension between data architects' instinct to build tightly coupled systems and the needs of distributed architectures, and reconcile service and data boundaries deliberately.
Make data-related architecture trade-offs by combining both an architecture-to-data and a data-to-architecture perspective.
Recognize that documenting a decision is a separate concern from governing its proper use, and pair every decision with a means of enforcement.
Choose fitness-function scope deliberately: use atomic functions for a single characteristic in isolation and holistic functions for interacting combinations of characteristics.
Allow fitness-function outputs to be context-dependent (dynamic) as long as the measure remains objective, for example performance per user as a function of concurrent users.
When meaningful options cannot be foreseen, adopt evolutionary architecture guided by a deliberately chosen fitness function instead of a fixed up-front design.
Account for synergy and conflict among architecture characteristics, since improving one (for example security) can degrade another (for example performance).

Protect modularity by automatically forbidding undesirable dependencies such as component cycles in the continuous build, because arbitrary cross-imports erode modularity and code reviews catch them too late.

Apply structural modifiability tactics deliberately: split a non-cohesive module into cohesive submodules, redistribute scattered similar responsibilities into one place (guided by likely change scenarios), and restrict dependencies via visibility restriction and authorization as in layering and wrappers.
Run fitness functions continually and automatically wherever possible, accepting the few that must be manual (such as legal review), because a validation that never runs validates nothing.
Use fitness functions as an executable checklist of important-but-not-urgent principles to prevent we-will-fix-it-later technical-debt slippage, without overusing them to frustrate teams.

Provide a shared governance slot in every team's deployment pipeline so security and governance checks, including zero-day responses, can be deployed and enforced universally instead of through error-prone manual sweeps.
Use a simple, shared definition of coupling as the basis for trade-off analysis: two artifacts are coupled if a change in one might require a change in the other.
Reject the advice to decouple maximally and instead apply coupling deliberately, because fully decoupled parts cannot collaborate and coupling is not inherently bad.

Adopt simple shared definitions for core terms (service, component, synchronous and asynchronous communication, orchestration and choreography, atomicity and eventual consistency, contract) to keep architecture discussions grounded and unambiguous.

Ground abstract architecture concepts against a concrete running example, preferably an existing (brownfield) system, because most real-world problems arise within existing systems rather than greenfield development.

Expect a large, reliability-troubled monolith to make change slow and risky and to fail all at once, and recognize that a single shared schema means data decomposition requires collaboration with the database team.
Untangle a distributed-architecture problem into its coupled dimensions and analyze them in isolation before reassembling, since no universal best practices apply to real-world complex systems.
Distinguish static coupling (how parts are wired together, often measurable at compile time) from dynamic coupling (how parts call one another at runtime, requiring continuous monitoring).

When no single tool can meet all of an application's storage and processing needs, decompose the work across best-fit tools integrated by application code, and make that application code responsible for upholding the composite system's guarantees such as keeping caches and indexes in sync and correctly invalidated.

When a configuration artifact can break production, add automated quality checks to the submit pipeline rather than forbidding changes, and at scale express configuration in a proper language with templates and functions, solving its problems with software tooling.
Prefer tolerating faults over preventing them, except where no cure exists (for example a security compromise or data leak that cannot be reversed), where prevention is the only option.

Reserve Byzantine fault tolerance for settings where nodes may be malicious or arbitrarily corrupted (such as aerospace or multi-organization systems), since it is usually unnecessary in a trusted single-organization datacenter and cannot save you from a bug deployed identically to all nodes or from a security compromise, but still add cheap pragmatic guards against weak forms of lying such as application-level checksums, input sanitization, and configuring multiple NTP servers.

Prevent faults proactively: use ACID transactions (often via two-phase commit) to stop race conditions, predictive models with monitors to act before a threshold is crossed, exception-prevention techniques like smart pointers and error-correcting codes, and increase a component's competence set so it raises fewer exceptions.

Limit the consequences of an unsafe state with containment tactics — abort an operation before it causes damage (fail-safe), degrade to maintain only the most critical functions in a planned safe way, and mask via voting with a simple reliable voter — and prevent propagation with barrier tactics such as firewall and interlock.

Account for hardware faults being largely random and independent while software faults are systematic, correlated across nodes, and cause more failures, and anticipate dormant bugs triggered when an environmental assumption stops holding.

Treat a system model's fault assumptions as probabilities rather than binary certainties, because rare violations such as on-disk corruption, network corruption evading checksums, and memory bit-flips do occur at scale, and because software bugs that lower-level checksums cannot catch occur even in mature databases and far more in application code.

Treat operator and configuration error as a leading cause of outages: minimize the opportunities for human error with well-designed abstractions and interfaces that make the right thing easy without being so restrictive that people work around them, and decouple mistake-prone places from places where mistakes cause failures by providing realistic sandboxes.

Never let a system simply crash on an exception: handle exceptions productively (from error codes to exception classes carrying name, origin, and cause) and detect altered control flow with tactics such as parameter fences, parameter typing, and timeouts.

Identify the true load parameter (which may not be the obvious request rate, as Twitter's fan-out shows), and when reads vastly outnumber writes precompute results at write time to make reads cheap, while watching for extreme high-fan-out entities that explode write cost and may need a hybrid read-time approach.

Treat response time as a distribution rather than a single number, report percentiles such as p50, p95, p99, and p999 instead of the mean, compute them efficiently with approximation algorithms over a rolling window, and never average percentiles (aggregate by adding histograms).

Set response-time targets at high percentiles (for example p999) and encode them in SLOs and SLAs because tail latencies shape user experience and often affect the most valuable customers, but avoid over-optimizing extreme percentiles like the 99.99th where random events dominate and returns diminish.

Account for queueing and head-of-line blocking dominating high-percentile latency by measuring response times on the client side, expect tail-latency amplification when one request fans out to multiple backend calls, and ensure load-test clients send requests independently of responses so queues are not artificially shortened.

Design for cloud long-tail latency, where a meaningful fraction of requests take far longer than the mean, by choosing the right statistic (not just the mean) and applying hedged or alternative requests that issue extra requests and cancel stragglers once enough responses arrive.

Use single-queue multiple-server designs to cut idling and frustration, and treat queues as valuable load buffers that only become harmful under excessive utilization, since high utilization and short response times do not mix.

Because most of software's cost is ongoing maintenance, design for operability, simplicity, and evolvability, and invest especially in operability since good operations can work around bad software but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations.

Choose a data model appropriate to the application because the model profoundly shapes both how the software is written and how its builders think about the problem; remember that applications layer models (each hiding the level below) and that every model embodies usage assumptions, making some operations easy and fast and others unsupported or awkward.

Understand the relational model as relations of unordered tuples that hide the internal data representation behind a clean interface, an approach that generalized far beyond its original scope while successive rival models generated hype but faded.

Expect an object-relational impedance mismatch when storing object-oriented data in relational tables (which ORMs reduce but do not eliminate), and prefer a document or JSON representation for self-contained one-to-many tree-structured data because it has better locality, fetching the whole record in one query instead of a multi-table shred and join.

When a human-meaningful value is referenced from many records, store an ID rather than duplicating the text, because the ID never needs to change and the meaningful information lives in one place, whereas duplication incurs write overhead and risks inconsistency; removing such duplication is the core idea of normalization.

Anticipate that normalization requires many-to-one relationships that fit the document model poorly (document databases support joins weakly, forcing you to emulate them in application code) and that data tends to become more interconnected as features are added, mirroring how the document model repeats the hierarchical model's weakness at many-to-many relationships.

Recognize that relational and document databases are not fundamentally different for many-to-one and many-to-many relationships (both reference related items by an identifier resolved at read time), and weigh the document model's advantages of schema flexibility, locality, and closeness to application structures against the relational model's stronger support for joins.

Prefer the relational model's open layout and automatic query optimizer over the manual access paths of the older hierarchical and network models, which made query and update code complicated and inflexible, recognizing the key insight that a general-purpose optimizer built once benefits every application and beats hand-coded access paths in the long run.

Query graphs with a declarative language such as Cypher or SPARQL that supports variable-length traversal and lets the optimizer choose the strategy, and avoid forcing graph queries into relational SQL, where the number of joins is not fixed in advance so recursive common table expressions become clumsy.

Do not mistake graph databases for a return of the CODASYL network model, because a graph database imposes no schema restricting which vertices connect, allows direct access to any vertex by id or index rather than mandatory access-path traversal, leaves vertices and edges unordered, and supports declarative query languages.

Choose the data model by the shape of the data's relationships: tree-structured or relationship-free data fits the document model (loaded as a whole, but unable to reference nested items directly), simple many-to-many fits the relational model, and highly interconnected data with common many-to-many relationships is most naturally a graph.

Use a graph data model (vertices and edges) when many-to-many relationships are common and connections are complex, taking advantage of the property graph's flexibility (any vertex can link to any other, with efficient bidirectional traversal and labeled edges) and its ability to store many different object types, even heterogeneous ones, in a single datastore.

Match the store to the relationship profile (document databases for self-contained data with rare relationships, graph databases when anything may relate to everything, relational in between), use the right specialized system rather than awkwardly emulating one model in another, remember that schema-free document and graph stores still rely on an implicit schema, and accept that some needs require purpose-built systems.

Prefer a declarative query language such as SQL, where you state the pattern of the results rather than how to compute them, over an imperative query API, because declarative queries are more concise, hide engine internals so performance can improve without query changes, and lend themselves to automatic optimization and parallel execution; the same advantage appears with declarative CSS or XPath versus imperative DOM manipulation.
Favor graphs when evolvability matters, because a graph can be extended with new vertex and edge types as features are added without restructuring existing data.

Treat the triple-store model as essentially equivalent to the property graph and independent of the overhyped, largely unrealized semantic web, recognizing that triples can be a good internal data model for applications even without publishing RDF.

Consider Datalog when queries are complex, since its rules derive new predicates from data or other rules and can be combined and reused across queries, which is less convenient for simple one-off queries but copes better with complex data.

Understand the B-tree as the dominant index structure: it breaks the database into fixed-size pages matching the disk's blocks, looks up a key by descending from a root page through key-range-bounded child references to a leaf, and stays balanced and shallow so few page reads are needed.

Recognize that B-tree writes overwrite pages in place, so multi-page operations risk a corrupted index on crash and are protected by a write-ahead log, that in-place updates require latch-based concurrency control, and that common optimizations include copy-on-write, abbreviated interior keys, and laying out leaf pages sequentially.

Weigh LSM-trees against B-trees by their characteristics rather than a fixed rule: LSM-trees usually sustain higher write throughput through sequential SSTable writes, lower write amplification, and better compression, but their background compaction can spike high-percentile latency or fail to keep up (so monitor it), while B-trees give faster, more predictable reads and keep each key in one place (attractive for transactional range locks); benchmark with your own workload to decide.

Use secondary indexes (crucial for efficient joins) understanding that an index value is either the row itself or a reference into an unordered heap file, and that a clustered index stores the row within the index while a covering index stores some columns to answer queries from the index alone, both speeding reads at the cost of extra storage and write overhead.

Remember that a concatenated index serves only queries on a leading prefix of its fields, and that querying several columns simultaneously (such as a geospatial latitude-longitude range) needs a multi-dimensional index like an R-tree or a space-filling curve rather than a standard one-dimensional B-tree or LSM-tree.

Do not expect exact-match indexes to find similar or misspelled keys; use dedicated fuzzy or full-text search techniques (such as synonym expansion, ignoring grammatical variants, and matching within a bounded edit distance) for that need.

Tolerate disks for their durability and lower cost per gigabyte, but consider an in-memory database when the dataset fits in memory, giving it durability through a disk change log, periodic snapshots, or replication, and recognizing that its speed comes from avoiding the overhead of encoding data for disk (not from avoiding disk reads) and that it can offer data models hard to implement on disk.

Distribute a database across machines for scalability, fault tolerance, or lower latency, choosing among shared-memory scale-up (limited by super-linear cost and a single location), shared-disk (limited by contention and locking overhead), and shared-nothing scale-out, which needs no special hardware, can span regions, and gives the best price-performance.

Model a data warehouse with a star schema, a central fact table whose rows are individual events surrounded by dimension tables, capturing facts as individual events for maximum analysis flexibility (accepting very large fact tables) and preferring star schemas over more normalized snowflake schemas because they are simpler for analysts.

Use column-oriented storage for analytic workloads, because row-oriented storage forces a query to load whole wide rows even when it touches only a few of many columns, whereas storing each column together lets a query read and parse only the columns it needs.

Exploit that column data compresses well (bitmap encoding plus run-length encoding, enabling fast bitwise filters) and that column storage enables vectorized processing in tight CPU-cache-friendly loops, while remembering that the column families of Cassandra and HBase are misleadingly named and remain mostly row-oriented.

Accept that column storage, compression, and sorting speed reads at the cost of harder writes (in-place update is impossible with compressed columns), and handle writes with an LSM-tree approach that buffers them in memory and merges them into the column files in bulk.

Use a materialized view (an actual on-disk copy of a query's results, unlike a virtual view) to cache expensive aggregates, but only where reads dominate (such as a data warehouse) because it must be updated on every underlying change and so makes writes more expensive; a data cube precomputes aggregates over dimensions for very fast queries but loses flexibility, so keep the raw data too.

Use a massively parallel processing relational database for demanding analytics, because its query optimizer breaks a complex query of joins, filters, grouping, and aggregation into stages and partitions that run in parallel across nodes, far beyond the single-key access of most NoSQL stores.

Understand that data travels a write path (work done eagerly when data is written) and a read path (work done only when queried) that meet at the derived dataset, and that caches, indexes, and materialized views shift that boundary, with no index meaning little write work but expensive read scans, precomputing all results being infeasible, and a cache of common queries being the practical middle ground.

Design data encodings for both forward compatibility (old code can read data written by new code) and backward compatibility (new code can read data written by old code), because both are needed to upgrade different parts of a system independently rather than all at once.

Treat data flowing through a database as requiring both backward and forward compatibility during rolling upgrades, preserve unknown fields when older code reads, updates, and rewrites a record, and avoid expensive migrations by remembering that data outlives code, persisting for years in its original encoding while application versions are replaced in minutes.

In tag-based formats like Protocol Buffers and Thrift, make every field added after initial deployment optional or give it a default, only remove fields that are optional, never reuse a tag number, and change a field's datatype only with care because it can lose precision or truncate values.

With Avro, rely on schema resolution that matches the writer's and reader's schemas by field name (they need only be compatible, not identical), only add or remove fields that have a default value, use union types to allow null (which is a valid default only as a union branch), and remember that renaming a field or adding a union branch is backward but not forward compatible.

Convey an Avro writer's schema by context, including it once at the start of a large file, recording a version number per record against a schema registry, or negotiating it on connection setup, and prefer Avro when schemas are dynamically generated because, having no tag numbers, it can be regenerated from a changing source schema with fields matched by name; a schema registry also serves as documentation and lets you check compatibility before deploying.

Prefer schema-based binary encodings over textual JSON, XML, or CSV when efficiency and evolvability matter, because they are more compact (field names can be omitted), the required schema serves as always-current documentation, a schema registry lets you check compatibility before deploying, and code generation gives compile-time type checking in statically typed languages.

Adopt rolling upgrades that deploy a new version to a few nodes at a time to release without downtime and reduce risk, which requires all data flowing through the system to be backward and forward compatible; among encoding formats, language-specific ones are weak on compatibility, textual ones depend on usage, and binary schema-driven ones give compact encoding with clear compatibility.

Select a data-interchange format by weighing expressiveness, interoperability (favor a standard like JSON), performance, implicit coupling, and transparency, understanding the verbosity-validation-versus-performance tradeoffs of XML, JSON, and Protocol Buffers.

Encode an archival snapshot once in the latest schema using an immutable, analytics-friendly format such as Avro object container files or columnar Parquet, since the snapshot is written in one go and thereafter immutable.

Choose REST for public APIs because, although a custom binary RPC protocol can be faster, REST is easy to experiment with and debug, universally supported, and rich in tooling; reserve RPC for intra-organization service calls, and manage RPC evolution by assuming servers are upgraded before clients (needing backward compatibility on requests and forward compatibility on responses) while maintaining cross-organization compatibility indefinitely through API versioning.

Understand the actor model as encapsulating concurrency in actors that each hold private state and communicate only by asynchronous messages whose delivery is not guaranteed, which avoids threads and locks and underlies distributed actor frameworks.

Replicate data to reduce latency, increase availability, and scale reads, recognizing that all the difficulty lies in handling changes and that leader-based replication has one leader accept all writes and stream its change log to followers, with clients reading from any replica but writing only to the leader.

Choose a replication synchrony level deliberately: synchronous replication guarantees an up-to-date follower but blocks all writes if that follower stops responding, fully asynchronous replication keeps the leader processing but can lose confirmed writes if the leader fails, so a semi-synchronous configuration with one synchronous follower and the rest asynchronous is the practical middle ground.

Treat leader failover (detecting failure by timeout, electing the most up-to-date replica, and reconfiguring clients) as hazardous, because asynchronous replication can lose the old leader's last writes, split brain can corrupt data, the failure-detection timeout is hard to tune, and discarded writes can desynchronize external systems, which is why some teams prefer manual failover and why node failures, unreliable networks, and the consistency-durability-availability-latency trade-offs are fundamental distributed-systems problems.

Use a read-scaling architecture that distributes read-only queries across many followers for read-heavy workloads (which realistically requires asynchronous replication), but account for asynchronous followers returning stale data and for eventual consistency being unbounded, since replication lag is usually sub-second yet can grow to minutes near capacity or during network problems.

Provide read-after-write consistency so users always see their own submitted updates, implementing it by reading anything the user may have modified from the leader or by tracking the user's last-write timestamp, and recognizing that doing so across a user's multiple devices is harder because the metadata must be centralized and requests may need routing to the same datacenter.

Reserve multi-leader replication (multiple nodes accepting writes, each a follower to the others) for cases where it pays off, such as multi-datacenter operation, offline-capable clients, and collaborative editing, rather than within a single datacenter where its benefits rarely outweigh the complexity; across datacenters it beats single-leader on write latency, datacenter-outage tolerance, and resilience to unreliable inter-datacenter links.

Treat write conflicts as the central downside of multi-leader replication and avoid the configuration where possible because it is often retrofitted and dangerous, recognizing that offline-capable clients are multi-leader replication taken to the extreme and that collaborative editing is a replication problem (document locking equals single-leader, small unlocked change units equal multi-leader requiring conflict resolution).

Understand leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication, where any replica accepts writes with no failover and reads and writes go to several nodes in parallel, and recover missed writes through read repair plus an anti-entropy background process, noting that without anti-entropy rarely-read values have reduced durability.

Configure leaderless quorums so that with n replicas a write needs w acknowledgements and a read queries r nodes with w + r > n to make the read and write sets overlap, and tune w and r as availability trade-offs (lowering them keeps reads or writes available when nodes are down, while skewing them favors fast reads or fast writes).

Across multiple leaderless replicas use a version vector (a version number per replica per key, each replica tracking the versions it has seen from the others) rather than a single version number, so the database can distinguish overwrites from concurrent writes and it is safe to read from one replica and write to another.

Default to single-leader replication when it suffices, because it is easy to understand and needs no conflict resolution, and turn to multi-leader or leaderless replication only when their robustness to faulty nodes, network interruptions, and latency spikes is worth the harder reasoning and weaker consistency guarantees.

Understand that a single-leader database concentrates decisions in the leader to provide linearizable operations, uniqueness constraints, and an ordered log but cannot progress if the leader fails, leaving three options (wait, fail over manually, or elect automatically), that having a leader does not avoid consensus but only defers it to maintaining leadership, and that if you need fault-tolerant consensus you should use a proven coordination service; theoretical results, even with unrealistic assumptions, are valuable for knowing what is possible.

Treat a database write as an event and the replication log as a stream of write events (so state machine replication is just event streaming), keep heterogeneous systems in sync not with error-prone dual writes but with change data capture that makes the source database the leader and derived data systems (caches, indexes, warehouses) its followers, implementing capture by parsing the replication log rather than fragile high-overhead triggers, and bootstrap a new derived system from a consistent snapshot taken at a known offset in the change log.

Set up a new follower without downtime by taking a consistent snapshot of the leader, copying it over, and replaying changes from the snapshot's exact log position until it has caught up, and let a follower recover from a crash or disconnection by requesting changes since the last position it recorded.

Provide monotonic reads so a user never sees time move backward (for example by routing each user's reads to the same replica) and consistent prefix reads so writes are observed in their causal order (by keeping causally related writes in the same partition or tracking causal dependencies).

Use total order broadcast for database replication (state machine replication, where every replica applies the same writes in the same order), taking advantage of its fixing the order at delivery (stronger than timestamp ordering) and its nature as an append-only log, and remember it is asynchronous so building writes on it yields linearizable writes but not linearizable reads, which need extra steps such as sequencing the read through the log or reading from a synchronously updated replica.

Build powerful processing by composing tools that each do one thing well (like the Unix sort utility, which spills to disk and parallelizes across cores), and choose between in-memory aggregation and sorting based on the working set, which equals the number of distinct keys: an in-memory hash table when it fits in memory, and disk-efficient sorting when it does not.

Treat perfect durability as unattainable and combine risk-reduction techniques (writing to disk, replicating to remote machines, and keeping backups) rather than trusting any single one, since disk-only data is inaccessible if the machine dies, correlated faults can knock out all replicas, asynchronous replication can lose recent writes, and disks and SSDs can corrupt or lose data.

Match the redundancy tactic to the fault class: exact replication only protects against random hardware failure, functional redundancy adds design diversity for common-mode failures (but not specification errors and at higher cost), and analytic redundancy with a sophisticated voter tolerates specification errors.

Use redundancy for safety where shutdown is undesirable, matching the type to the fault: replication for random hardware faults, functional redundancy for common-mode failures, and analytic redundancy that partitions the system into a simple high-assurance portion and a complex high-performance portion.

Exploit that a transaction can abort and be safely retried, but handle the imperfections of retrying: deduplicate when a commit's acknowledgment is lost to avoid double execution, back off and limit retries under overload, retry only transient errors, beware side effects outside the database, and account for a client dying mid-retry.

Achieve exactly-once handling of retried operations primarily through idempotence, recognizing that TCP duplicate suppression works only within a single connection (so a non-idempotent transfer can run twice on retry) and that database-level deduplication does not cover the network between the end-user device and the server, so you need an end-to-end operation identifier passed all the way to the database.

Do not trust isolation-level names to tell you the actual guarantee, because snapshot isolation is called serializable in Oracle and repeatable read in PostgreSQL and MySQL, and the SQL standard's ambiguous definitions mean databases claiming the same level provide widely differing protection.

To make two-phase locking serializable it must prevent phantoms with predicate locks over a search condition, but because predicate locks perform poorly when many are active, most databases use index-range (next-key) locking as a safe over-approximation that locks a larger set attached to an index entry.

Recognize that a timeout is the only sure way to detect a node fault yet has no simple right value (too long delays recovery, too short falsely declares slow nodes dead), that prematurely declaring a live node dead is harmful (double-executed actions and load that can cascade), and that real asynchronous networks are unbounded so a transient round-trip spike can mislead a low timeout.

Choose timeouts experimentally from the measured round-trip-time distribution, because packet-delay variability comes mostly from queueing and is worst near capacity and because a noisy neighbor in a shared cloud can make delays highly variable, and prefer adaptive timeouts that continually measure response times and jitter (as a Phi Accrual failure detector does) over fixed constants.

Do not expect hard real-time guarantees in ordinary server systems, since meeting a deadline in all circumstances requires a real-time operating system, documented worst-case execution times, and extensive testing that is expensive and restrictive; instead mitigate process pauses pragmatically (for example treating a garbage-collection pause as a planned outage by draining and restarting a node), and accept that a node cannot know anything for certain because a non-responding node's state is unknowable.

Insert a circuit breaker to stop endless retries against a faulty component and prevent cascading failures, and tune its timeout/retry values carefully because too long adds latency while too short causes false-positive trips.

Use timeouts to detect failure in distributed systems but recognize they cannot distinguish a real failure from a slow reply, cannot localize failure, and can falsely trigger on accumulated slow responses, so parameterize detection by timeout interval and number of missed responses over a window and tune it to the network, relaxing it for wide-area, cellular, or satellite links.

Choose UDP when delayed data is worthless (such as voice or video) because it trades reliability for lower delay variability by skipping flow control and retransmission, and understand that variable network delay is not a law of nature but the consequence of dynamic resource partitioning, which packet-switched networks use for efficiency in contrast to the bounded delay of reserved-bandwidth circuits.

Do not rely on rapid feedback that a remote node is down (a TCP acknowledgment, ICMP message, or switch interface), because even a delivered packet may not have been handled if the application crashed, so confirm success only with a positive response from the application itself.

Account for time being hard in distributed systems, because variable message delay makes a message's send-to-receive gap unknown and event ordering across machines uncertain, and because each machine has its own imperfect quartz clock that drifts and is only approximately synchronized by NTP.

Reason with explicit system models, choosing among timing models (synchronous with bounded delay, partially synchronous most of the time, or asynchronous with no timing assumptions) and node-failure models (crash-stop, crash-recovery, or Byzantine), and use the partially synchronous model with crash-recovery faults as the most realistic for real systems.

Reason about performance by characterizing the events that can occur and when, and the system's time-based response, treating processing time and blocked time as the two basic contributors and identifying where resource limitations significantly contribute to latency.

Assume clock error between devices (hardware drift and NTP limits) and design distributed systems so correct functioning does not require time synchronization; when order matters more than time, use mechanisms such as vector clocks to establish happened-before rather than comparing clock times.

Measure durations and timeouts with a monotonic clock rather than a time-of-day clock (which can jump backward on reset and ignores leap seconds), and treat clock synchronization as unreliable given quartz drift, forced resets, NTP's network-bounded accuracy, leap seconds, and virtual-machine clock jumps; very high accuracy is achievable with GPS and the Precision Time Protocol but is costly and fragile.

Write software to be robust against incorrect clocks just as against faulty networks, because a defective clock or misconfigured NTP usually goes unnoticed and causes silent data loss, and if the software requires synchronized clocks, monitor the clock offsets between machines and declare any node whose clock drifts too far as dead.

Do not use time-of-day timestamps to order events across nodes, because even sub-millisecond skew lets last-write-wins silently drop a causally later write, and NTP cannot be made accurate enough since its accuracy is bounded by network round-trip time; instead use logical clocks (incrementing counters) to capture ordering and treat any physical clock reading as a confidence interval rather than a point.

Expect a global monotonically increasing transaction ID across partitions to be hard to generate, because it requires coordination that reflects causality and becomes an untenable bottleneck under many small transactions.

Make a distributed system reliable by stating its fault assumptions as an explicit system model and designing to meet them, since algorithms can be proven correct within a model, but remember the model is a simplification, so the implementation must still handle cases the model assumes cannot happen, and combine theoretical proof with empirical testing because a proof does not guarantee correct real behavior.

Treat partial failures as the defining characteristic of distributed systems and build tolerance for them, while recognizing that detecting faults is hard because most systems rely on timeouts that cannot distinguish a network failure from a node failure and a degraded limping node can be even harder to handle than a cleanly failed one.

Define truth by the majority rather than any single node's judgment, using a majority quorum of more than half the nodes for decisions including declaring a node dead, which tolerates failures while staying safe because there can be only one majority at a time.

Hold a consensus algorithm to its four properties (uniform agreement, integrity, validity, and termination), recognizing that without fault tolerance consensus is trivial via a dictator node whose failure halts all decisions (the two-phase-commit problem), that termination requires a majority of nodes working, and that the safety properties of agreement, integrity, and validity hold even if a majority fails.

Enforce that there is only one of something (one leader, lock holder, or username owner) carefully, because a node believing it is the chosen one does not mean a quorum agrees, and protect a locked resource with fencing tokens, a monotonically increasing number the lock server returns and every write carries, where the resource itself actively rejects any write bearing a stale token.

Distinguish safety properties (nothing bad happens, with an identifiable and irreversible violation) from liveness properties (something good eventually happens), requiring safety to hold in all situations of the system model while allowing liveness to be conditioned on caveats such as a majority surviving and the network eventually recovering.

Never rely on a single sensor for safety-critical decisions when redundant sensors are available, and always test safety-critical software under sensor-failure conditions, because such single-sensor untested designs are implicated in real fatal accidents.

Enumerate the ways unsafe states arise (omission, commission, timing, incorrect values, sequence omission/commission, out-of-sequence) and respond by recovering and continuing, entering a safe mode, failing safe, or switching to manual, always reporting and/or logging the unsafe state immediately.

Specify safety requirements as scenarios whose stimulus is an omission, commission, incorrect data, or timing/sequence failure and whose measures include the percentage of unsafe states avoided or recovered, change in risk exposure (loss size times probability), and time in degraded, safe, or shutdown mode.

Prefer keeping things on a single machine when you can, since distribution brings partial failures, unreliable clocks, and process pauses, and adopt a distributed system only when scalability, fault tolerance, or low latency genuinely require it; note that supercomputers must stop and restart entirely on a component failure whereas distributed systems can run continuously by handling faults at the node level.

Understand linearizability as a recency guarantee that makes a system appear to have a single copy of the data on which operations take effect atomically, distinct from serializability (a multi-object transaction isolation property), and remember that two-phase locking and serial execution are typically linearizable while serializable snapshot isolation is not.

Accept the fundamental cost of linearizability under network partitions, where requiring it makes disconnected replicas unavailable while not requiring it keeps each replica available but non-linearizable, recognizing this applies to any linearizable database on an unreliable network (the essence of CAP), that CAP's pick-two-of-three framing is misleading and best avoided, and that giving each partition its own leader does not affect single-object linearizability.

Do not assume systems are linearizable (even multi-core RAM is not without memory barriers), since linearizability is usually dropped for performance rather than fault tolerance and is provably slow because its read and write response time is at least proportional to network-delay uncertainty, so weaker consistency models can be much faster.

Recognize that linearizability is appealing because it makes a database behave like a single-threaded variable but is slow under network delays, and that a wide range of problems are equivalent and reducible to consensus (linearizable compare-and-set, atomic transaction commit, total order broadcast, locks and leases, membership services, and uniqueness constraints), so identifying that a need reduces to consensus tells you what machinery it requires.

Require linearizability where correctness depends on a single agreed value, such as locking and leader election or a hard uniqueness constraint, but do not impose it where it is unneeded, since foreign-key and attribute constraints can be enforced without it and some constraints can be interpreted loosely and corrected after the fact.

Watch for cross-channel timing dependencies, where two communication channels connecting the same components (such as a file store plus a message queue) create a race condition unless the shared storage is linearizable, and use linearizable storage or an equivalent coordinating approach to close the race.

Reason about ordering through causality, which orders cause before effect and defines a partial order in which concurrent operations are incomparable, in contrast to linearizability's total order, and note that linearizability is stronger than and implies causal consistency, automatically preserving causality even across multiple communication channels.

Prefer causal consistency when you need ordering guarantees without linearizability's cost, because it is the strongest consistency model that does not slow down under network delays and stays available during network failures (the CAP trade-off does not apply), maintaining it by having a replica process an operation only after all operations that causally precede it.

Order events with compact sequence numbers or logical clocks rather than tracking every causal dependency, knowing that a single-leader replication log already gives a causal total order, that ad hoc generators (per-node odd/even numbers, physical-clock timestamps, or preallocated blocks) are not consistent with causality, and that Lamport timestamps give a causality-consistent total order by propagating the maximum counter value seen.

Treat a linearizable compare-and-set register, total order broadcast, and consensus as equivalent problems so a solution to one solves the others, and understand consensus as getting nodes to agree on something, which is deceptively hard, and that the FLP impossibility holds only in the asynchronous model so allowing timeouts or randomness makes consensus solvable in practice.

Use a proven coordination service such as ZooKeeper or etcd, which provides linearizable atomic operations, total ordering with fencing tokens, failure detection, and change notifications over fault-tolerant total order broadcast, for tasks like leader election with automatic failover and assigning partitions to nodes, rather than implementing a consensus system yourself, which is hard to get right.

Understand that single-node atomic commit hinges on the order data is durably written (data first, then the commit record, whose durable write is the deciding moment) and that a commit must be irrevocable because once data is committed it becomes visible and other transactions may rely on it.

Understand two-phase commit as achieving atomic commit across nodes via a coordinator that asks participants to prepare and promise, then durably records its decision and tells everyone to commit or abort (distinct from two-phase locking), with atomicity resting on two points of no return (a participant's yes vote and the coordinator's logged decision), and recognize it is a blocking protocol because a coordinator crash leaves participants in doubt and unable to decide alone.

Do not expect three-phase commit to fix two-phase commit in practice, since it assumes bounded delay and response times that real systems lack, so two-phase commit persists despite its coordinator-failure problem; weigh distributed transactions' mixed reputation and heavy performance cost, and distinguish database-internal transactions (which often work well) from heterogeneous ones across different technologies (which are much harder).

Understand total order broadcast as equivalent to repeated rounds of consensus (each decision delivering one message in agreed order) and single-leader replication as total order broadcast whose manual leader is a dictator-style consensus that fails termination, so fault-tolerant automatic leader election itself requires consensus.

Recognize that consensus protocols break the leader-election circularity with epoch numbering, giving each election a monotonically increasing epoch with a unique leader (a higher epoch winning conflicts), and use two rounds of voting (to elect a leader and to approve each proposal) whose quorums overlap so a leader can confirm no higher epoch exists before deciding.

Account for the real costs of consensus, namely that its proposal voting is synchronous replication, that it requires a strict majority so a network split blocks the minority side, that most algorithms assume a fixed membership, and that timeout-based leader-failure detection in variable networks can cause frequent leader elections that wreck performance.

Use a coordination service like ZooKeeper (which runs a small fixed quorum of three or five nodes voting among themselves while serving many clients) for small, slow-changing coordination data such as which node leads a partition, not for fast-changing application state; remember that service discovery does not actually require consensus (DNS suffices) while a membership service couples failure detection with consensus so nodes agree on who is alive.

Do not build distributed coordination yourself: shared-data coordination is hard because two-phase commit needs multiple fallible messages and lock holders can fail, and consensus algorithms like Paxos are notoriously hard to implement correctly, so use a proven package such as ZooKeeper, Consul, or etcd.

Expect real applications to integrate several datastores, indexes, caches, and analytics systems because no single database fits all access patterns, and bring clarity by distinguishing systems of record (the authoritative, normalized source of truth) from derived data (redundant copies recreatable from the source and kept for read performance), recognizing the distinction depends on how a store is used rather than the tool itself.

Classify a data system as an online service, a batch process, or a stream process according to its performance priority (response time, throughput, or low-latency derived output), and apply the Unix philosophy, which transfers to large-scale data systems: make each program do one thing well, expect each program's output to become another's input, and build software to be tried early and rebuilt.

Recognize that databases, Hadoop, and operating systems all fundamentally store and process data (Unix offering low-level abstractions and relational databases high-level ones), that running CREATE INDEX reprocesses the dataset into a derived view much like bootstrapping change data capture, and that an entire organization's dataflow can be seen as one huge database whose batch, stream, and ETL processes act like the subsystems maintaining indexes and materialized views.

Enable composability with a uniform interface (the Unix file, an ordered byte sequence, lets files, pipes, sockets, and devices interoperate), separate logic from wiring by reading standard input and writing standard output so the shell can compose programs with loose coupling, and preserve transparency for experimentation by treating inputs as immutable, allowing intermediate output to be inspected, and letting later stages restart without rerunning the whole pipeline.

Understand MapReduce as a distributed Unix-like job that does not modify its input and writes output once, running on HDFS, a shared-nothing filesystem with a central NameNode tracking blocks and per-machine daemons, which tolerates faults by replicating blocks (as full copies or via erasure coding) and schedules computation near the data for locality when network bandwidth is the bottleneck.

Account for the MapReduce shuffle (each mapper partitions its output by reducer using a hash of the key, writes sorted files, and reducers fetch and merge their partition) and for chaining single jobs into workflows where one job's output directory becomes the next job's input directory.

Remember that MapReduce has no indexes and reads its entire input as a full table scan, which is reasonable for analytic aggregates but outrageously expensive for fetching a few records, and never query a remote database once per record in a batch job (which limits throughput, can overwhelm the database, and makes the job nondeterministic); instead copy the data into the same distributed filesystem and join it locally.

Treat Hadoop as a distributed version of Unix (HDFS as the filesystem, MapReduce as a process that sorts between map and reduce) and exploit that distributed-filesystem files are just byte sequences in any encoding, so you can dump raw data into storage and decide how to interpret it later (schema-on-read, the data lake), making data available quickly rather than insisting on up-front modeling.

Use higher-level models like Pig, Hive, Cascading, or Crunch instead of the raw MapReduce APIs (where you must write join algorithms from scratch), and be aware that MapReduce fully materializes intermediate state to the distributed filesystem, which compared to Unix pipes forces a job to wait for all preceding tasks, creates redundant mapper reads, and replicates temporary data unnecessarily.

Prefer a dataflow engine such as Spark, Tez, or Flink, which treats a whole workflow as one job of connected operators that sort only where needed, avoid redundant map tasks, optimize for locality, keep intermediate state in memory or on local disk, and reuse JVM processes, so it usually runs the same computations significantly faster than MapReduce while letting existing high-level code switch engines with a configuration change.

Exploit that MapReduce and its dataflow successors differ from fully declarative SQL by running arbitrary callback code with access to existing libraries (their flexibility advantage over MPP databases), while incorporating declarative features beyond joins lets the optimizer use column-oriented storage and vectorized execution, so the frameworks approach MPP performance without losing the ability to run arbitrary code over arbitrary formats.

Prefer a map-side join (no reducers or sorting, each mapper reading one block and writing one file) when input properties allow it, using a broadcast hash join when one input fits in memory, a partitioned hash join when both inputs are identically partitioned, and a merge join when they are also sorted, while remembering that the join choice affects the output's partitioning and sorting so you must know the datasets' physical layout to optimize.

Use high-level dataflow APIs (Hive, Pig, Spark, Flink) that express computations with relational building blocks, and specify joins declaratively so a cost-based optimizer can choose the most suitable join algorithm and reorder joins to minimize intermediate state, sparing you from remembering all the join algorithms.

Anticipate that bringing all records for one key to the same place breaks down for hot keys (where one reducer is overloaded and the job waits for it), and mitigate the skew with a skewed or sharded join that spreads a hot key's records across several random reducers while replicating the other input, or with two-stage grouping.

Build derived datasets like search indexes with batch processing (mappers partition the documents and each reducer builds an immutable index for its partition), and to publish a batch job's output do not write to the production database one record at a time from a mapper or reducer (which is slow, can overwhelm the database, and breaks the all-or-nothing guarantee), but instead build a brand-new immutable database as files in the job's output directory and bulk-load it into read-only servers.

Gain human fault tolerance by treating batch inputs as immutable, fully replacing previous output, and avoiding side effects, so that buggy code can be fixed and the job rerun (or the old output directory switched back to), which a read-write transactional database cannot offer.

Rely on the deliberately restricted batch programming model, where stateless callbacks have no externally visible side effects beyond their output, to let the framework hide distributed-systems problems by safely retrying tasks and making the output as if no faults occurred, and remember that a batch job is distinguished by reading bounded, fixed-size input so it eventually completes, unlike an unbounded stream.

Treat batch and stream processing as functional pipelines of deterministic operations over immutable inputs (stream processing adding managed fault-tolerant state), and maintain derived data systems asynchronously and loosely coupled rather than synchronously, because asynchrony contains a fault locally whereas synchronous distributed transactions amplify failures across the system.

Recognize that dataflow engines tolerate faults by recomputing lost state from tracked lineage rather than from durable files, which requires operators to be deterministic (or downstream operators must be killed and rerun), and that recomputation is not always best, since materializing intermediate data to files is cheaper when that data is small relative to the source or the computation is CPU-intensive.

Expect dataflow engines to execute in a pipelined manner, incrementally passing an operator's output onward without waiting for its input to complete, except that any sorting operation must consume its entire input before producing output, with the job's final result still written to durable storage.

Recognize that keeping an immutable history forever is feasible for add-mostly workloads but problematic for high-update-and-delete workloads on small datasets, where the history grows large and compaction performance becomes crucial, and that you may be required to truly delete data for administrative or privacy reasons, which is hard because copies persist in storage engines, SSDs, and backups.

Choose the right window type for stream aggregation (tumbling, hopping, sliding, or session) and the right stream-join type (stream-stream, stream-table, or table-table), recognizing that stream joins are harder than batch joins because new events can arrive at any time and all three require the processor to maintain state derived from one input and query it on the other.

Implement a stream-stream join by maintaining recent events keyed by the join key within a time window, a stream-table (enrichment) join by keeping a local copy of the table up to date via change data capture rather than querying a remote database per event, and a table-table join by maintaining a materialized view from two changelog streams (such as a Twitter timeline cache from tweet and follow events).

Treat unbundling as complementary to, not a replacement for, databases (which are still needed for stream-processor state and serving query outputs) and as a way to gain breadth across many workloads rather than depth, so if one product already does everything you need you should simply use it; note that a high-level declarative language for wiring storage and processing systems together (an unbundled-database shell) is still missing.
